meta.blurb: A wireless message warns a ship full of passengers that the famous thief Arsène Lupin is on board. But which of them is he? In nine adventures, this charming gentleman-burglar robs the rich and makes Inspector Ganimard look foolish.
meta.bible: Arsène Lupin: the gentleman-burglar, a master of disguises, charming, daring and fond of a joke; he also appears as Bernard d'Andrézy, Guillaume Berlat, Jean Daspry, Horace Velmont and Grimaudan. Inspector Ganimard: the old, patient detective who arrests Lupin and never quite catches him. Monsieur Dudouis: Chief of the Sûreté. The Arrest of Arsène Lupin: La Provence, a liner crossing to New York. Miss Nelly Underdown: a rich, kind young woman. Lady Jerland: her friend. Monsieur Rozaine: a pale, fair-haired passenger. Major Rawson. Arsène Lupin in Prison: Baron Nathan Cahorn lives alone in the Château de Malaquis, a castle on a rock in the Seine, with his Rubens and Watteau paintings. Caudebec: the nearby town. Prison de la Santé: the Paris prison. The Escape of Arsène Lupin: Inspectors Dieuzy and Folenfant. Judge Jules Bouvier. Désiré Baudru: a poor man who looks a little like Lupin. Bois de Boulogne: the park in Paris. The Mysterious Traveller: Madame Renaud, a nervous lady; Rouen; Pierre Onfrey, a wanted criminal; the policemen Massol and Delivet; Darnétal. The Queen's Necklace: the Count and Countess de Dreux-Soubise; Henriette, a poor friend of the countess; her small son Raoul; the Chevalier Floriani. The Seven of Hearts: Jean Daspry; Georges Andermatt, a banker, and Madame Andermatt; the brothers Etienne and Alfred Varin; the engineer Louis Lacombe; Salvator, a mystery writer in the newspaper Echo de France; Neuilly. Madame Imbert's Safe: Ludovic Imbert and Gervaise Imbert; André Brawford. The Black Pearl: the Countess d'Andillot, once the singer Léotine Zalti; Victor Danègre, her servant; Mademoiselle de Sinclèves; avenue Hoche; Parc Monceau; Montmartre. Sherlock Holmes Arrives Too Late: the Château de Thibermesnil near Dieppe; the banker Georges Devanne; Father Gélis; Sherlock Holmes, the English detective; Duke Rollo; Sully; King Louis the Sixteenth; Hall of the Guards; Tour Guillaume. Paris. France. America. New York. Chicago. England. Voice and tone: light, quick and witty, full of cunning plans and elegant jokes; thefts are never violent, and every deed ends with a surprise. Additional names and facts. The Arrest of Arsène Lupin: Bernard d'Andrézy is the false name under which Lupin travels and tells the story; the Marquis de Raverdan, secretary to the American Ambassador; Rivolta, an Italian with a heavy black beard; Louis Rozaine, son of a rich Bordeaux merchant; Underdown of Chicago, Nelly's father; Kodak, the camera; the Atlantic; Le Havre; Baron Schormann. Arsène Lupin in Prison: Château de Malaquis; Baron Satan, the Baron's nickname on the Bourse; Philippe de Champaigne; Rubens; Watteau; Jean Goujon; Beauvais; Jacob; Batignolles station; Réveil de Caudebec; Echo de France; Rouen; Procureur; Jumièges; Agnès Sorel; Charles the Seventh; Seine; Dudouis; rue Pergolèse; Jules Bouvier. The Escape of Arsène Lupin: Prison de la Santé; Dépôt; Grand Journal; Argus de la Presse; Henry Clay; Carlyle; Epictetus; Leyden; Maître Danval; boulevard Saint-Michel; quai de l'Horloge; Palais de Justice; Soufflot; Port-Royal; Baudru; Désiré Baudru; Bois de Boulogne; Auteuil; La Muette; Châtelet; Doctor Altier; Saint-Louis Hospital; Bertillon; Courbevoie; Asnières; Levallois; Ternes; the British Ambassador. The Mysterious Traveller: Guillaume Berlat; Madame Renaud; Georges Ardelle; Saint-Lazare; Rouen; Darnétal; Montérolier-Buchy; Amiens; Honoré Massol; Gaston Delivet; Moreau-Lepton; Pierre Onfrey; rue Lafontaine; Buchy. The Queen's Necklace: Gaston de Dreux-Soubise; Böhmer and Bassenge, court jewellers; Madame Du Barry; Cardinal de Rohan; Marie-Antoinette; Jeanne de la Motte; Rétaux de Villette; Jeffreys, an English jeweller; Palais de Castille; King Christian; faubourg Saint-Germain; commissary Valorbe; Anquety; Péchard; Chevalier Floriani; Marquis de Rouzières; president of Essaville; deputy Bochas; Palermo; Crédit Lyonnais; Suresnes. The Seven of Hearts: Jean Daspry; Antoine, the servant; boulevard Maillot; Neuilly; Gil Blas; Cascade restaurant; the Saint-Martins; Louis Lacombe; Seven-of-Hearts, the submarine; Georges Andermatt, founder of the Metal Exchange; rue de Berry; Madame Andermatt; Etienne Varin; Alfred Varin; Lausanne; Salvator; Major von Lieben; Minister of Marine. Madame Imbert's Safe: boulevard Berthier; avenue de la Grande-Armée; Courcelles; Porte-Maillot; Montmartre; Place de l'Etoile; André Brawford. The Black Pearl: avenue Hoche; Doctor Harel; Léotine Zalti; Count d'Andillot; Victor Danègre; Anatole Dufour; Mademoiselle de Sinclèves; Grimaudan; locksmith Outard; rue Oberkampf; Bazar de la République; Parc Monceau; rue Lepic; Courcelles. Sherlock Holmes Arrives Too Late: Horace Velmont, Lupin's name as a painter; Georges Devanne and his mother; cousin d'Estevan; Monsieur and Madame d'Androl; Edouard, the chauffeur; Chronique de Thibermesnil; Tour Guillaume; Louise de Tancarville; Duke Edgard; Henry the Fourth; Sully; Royales Economies d'Etat; Louis the Sixteenth; Geoffroy; Arques; Halleux; Roquefort; Colonel Beauvel; Aubusson; Fragonard; Nattier; Houdon; Louvre; Iron Casket; Dieppe; Normandy; Benedictine; Hall of the Guards; the motto Fais ce que veulx. Montigny; Gruchet; Crasville; Roquefort; Louis the Fifteenth; Nelly's white rose.
chapters: The Painter Who Looks Like Lupin

beats.scene: A fast ocean liner sails across a calm sea under a bright sky
beats.summary: The liner La Provence sails for New York with a friendly captain and a cheerful company of passengers, cut off from the world as if on an island.

beats.scene: A wireless operator listens at his machine as lightning flashes outside
beats.summary: In a violent storm on the second day, the wireless warns the ship that Arsène Lupin is on board, until a flash of lightning cuts off the message.

beats.scene: Passengers whisper in little groups on the deck and in the smoking room
beats.summary: The secret spreads at once, and everyone remembers the famous thief, the card he left at Baron Schormann's house, and his many disguises.

beats.scene: A beautiful young woman talks to a gentleman beside the deck chairs
beats.summary: Miss Nelly Underdown, a rich young woman going to join her father in Chicago, asks Bernard d'Andrézy whether he has learned anything.

beats.scene: Two passengers sit in deck chairs in the sunshine after the storm
beats.summary: Bernard admires Nelly and notices a quiet young rival; he suggests that the passengers can solve the mystery as well as the detective Ganimard.

beats.scene: A man runs his finger down a passenger list on a sunny deck
beats.summary: From the clues of fair hair, a name beginning with R and travelling alone, Bernard studies the list: thirteen men with an R, and only four of them alone.

beats.scene: An Italian with a thick black beard laughs among a group of passengers
beats.summary: Raverdan, Rawson and the black-bearded Rivolta are quickly cleared, which leaves a fair-haired man named Rozaine, who has said nothing.

beats.scene: A pale young man rolls up a sleeve to show his bare arm
beats.summary: Rozaine says calmly that he fits every clue; asked about the wound, he shows his arm, but it is the left arm and not the right.

beats.scene: A woman runs along a ship's deck holding an empty jewel case
beats.summary: Lady Jerland rushes up crying that her jewels have been stolen: the thief has taken her finest stones and left the mountings.

beats.scene: Empty jewelled mountings lie on a table in a ship's cabin
beats.summary: The theft was done in daylight in a busy corridor; the passengers all blame Lupin, and that evening they hear that Rozaine has been arrested.

beats.scene: Couples dance on a ship's deck under a bright full moon
beats.summary: That night the passengers dance again and Bernard declares his love to Nelly under the moon, but next morning Rozaine is free: his papers are in order.

beats.scene: A pale man walks alone while two women rise and leave a table
beats.summary: Rozaine's enemies say Lupin could forge any papers, and nobody else fits the clues; when he comes towards the group Nelly and Lady Jerland walk away.

beats.scene: Sailors and stewards read a handwritten notice pinned to a board
beats.summary: Rozaine offers ten thousand francs for the discovery of Lupin and promises to unmask him himself; the captain searches the ship from end to end.

beats.scene: A man shows a small camera to a young woman on deck
beats.summary: Bernard shows Nelly his Kodak, in which a thief could hide all the jewels; soon afterwards the captain's watch vanishes and turns up in an officer's collar box.

beats.scene: A bound man lies in a dark corner of the ship's deck
beats.summary: An officer finds Rozaine tied with a scarf over his head; a card says that Lupin gladly accepts his ten thousand francs, and twenty thousand have been taken.

beats.scene: Passengers cling together in a ship's lounge, looking anxiously around
beats.summary: Nobody dares to stay alone; on the last day the passengers fear a worse crime, and Nelly seeks Bernard's protection, which delights him.

beats.scene: A liner with a long gangway lies beside a crowded pier in New York
beats.summary: At New York the customs officers come aboard and Nelly, pale and nervous, points out with Bernard a small old man with an umbrella: Ganimard.

beats.scene: A small old man with an umbrella lets one passenger pass and stops another
beats.summary: Ganimard lets Rozaine pass; Bernard gives Nelly his camera, and before they have gone ten steps Ganimard bars the way and asks if he is Lupin.

beats.scene: A policeman grips a man's arm while a young woman walks down the gangway
beats.summary: Ganimard strikes the unhealed wound and Bernard surrenders; Nelly, understanding everything, carries the camera down the gangway and lets it fall into the water.

beats.scene: A man stands in handcuffs on a ship's deck looking at the water
beats.summary: Lupin sighs that he is not an honest man; years later he tells the story himself, saying he can never describe his own face.

beats.scene: A small stone castle stands on a rock in the middle of a river
beats.summary: In Arsène Lupin in Prison, the little castle of Malaquis stands on a rock in the Seine, joined to the shore by a bridge, with a stormy past and a legend of a secret tunnel.

beats.scene: A stout old baron bars the iron gates of a castle bridge at sunset
beats.summary: Baron Nathan Cahorn, nicknamed Baron Satan on the Bourse, lives alone with three old servants among his Rubens, his Watteau paintings and his other treasures.

beats.scene: A postman hands a registered letter to an old man on a bridge
beats.summary: One Thursday in September a postman brings the baron a registered letter, the first he has had in years, headed Prison de la Santé and signed Arsène Lupin.

beats.scene: A baron reads a letter on a bridge with a frightened face
beats.summary: Lupin writes that he admires the Champaigne, the Rubens, the smallest Watteau and other treasures, and asks for them within eight days, or he will come on the night of 27 September.

beats.scene: A baron writes at a desk by candlelight, glancing at a stern castle wall
beats.summary: The exact knowledge of the castle alarms the baron; he writes to the prosecutor at Rouen, who says Lupin is closely guarded, though an expert finds certain resemblances in the writing.

beats.scene: A newspaper lies open on a table beside a worried baron and a map
beats.summary: Two days later the baron reads in the Réveil de Caudebec that the detective Ganimard is on holiday in the town, and the editor points out a little fisherman.

beats.scene: A little fisherman in a straw hat ignores a worried baron on a quay
beats.summary: Ganimard listens without moving, says that thieves do not warn their victims and that nobody has ever escaped from the Santé, and tells the baron not to frighten the fish.

beats.scene: A boy hands a telegram to a fisherman sitting on a campstool
beats.summary: On 26 September a telegram arrives from Lupin; the baron rushes back to Caudebec and offers three thousand francs, and Ganimard agrees to come with two of his men.

beats.scene: Two big men stand in a dim gallery while a small man holds keys
beats.summary: On the night, Ganimard barricades the doors, locks his two assistants in the central gallery and waits with the baron in the watchman's room, where he sleeps through a distant horn.

beats.scene: Two big men sleep on chairs in a gallery with bare walls
beats.summary: At dawn the baron is radiant, but in the gallery the two assistants are asleep, and the paintings, tapestries and jewels have vanished, leaving only nails and cords.

beats.scene: Gendarmes and reporters crowd into an old castle hall
beats.summary: The famous detective is stunned: nothing is broken and the assistants have been drugged, probably by the water in the carafe; the baron offers any price for his treasures and files a complaint against Lupin.

beats.scene: Newspaper reporters and gendarmes crowd into the rooms of an old castle
beats.summary: The castle fills with officials and reporters, the Echo de France prints Lupin's letter, the police hunt in vain for tunnels, and Dudouis sends for Ganimard.

beats.scene: A detective speaks earnestly to his chief in a Paris office
beats.summary: Ganimard says the solution lies with Lupin, a modern cracksman who uses no old tricks, and asks permission to spend an hour in his cell.

beats.scene: A smiling prisoner greets a small detective in a bare cell
beats.summary: Lupin welcomes Ganimard like an old friend, apologises for the hard stool and lack of beer, complains of the spies who search him, and recalls the Cahorn affair.

beats.scene: A prisoner opens the drawer of a small white wooden table
beats.summary: Lupin says he managed the whole affair from beginning to end and takes the receipts for the letter and the telegram from his drawer, to Ganimard's astonishment.

beats.scene: A prisoner paces his cell explaining with sweeping gestures
beats.summary: Lupin explains that the letter was needed to set the machine going: a castle that cannot be entered must invite the thief, and a frightened owner will ask the first detective he hears of.

beats.scene: A prisoner laughs while a puzzled detective bites his lip
beats.summary: A friend posed as Ganimard at Caudebec; the baron swallowed the bait, and while the false detective kept him busy two men lowered the treasures into a launch.

beats.scene: A detective cracks an egg and finds a small blue paper inside
beats.summary: At lunch Lupin says the baron has probably recovered his goods; Ganimard breaks an egg and finds a telegram: Contract closed, hundred thousand balls delivered.

beats.scene: A prisoner smiles as he leans toward a detective in a small cell
beats.summary: The balls are francs; Ganimard admits that the police could not bear a dozen such men, and Lupin promises that he will not be present at his own trial.

beats.scene: A detective at a prison door as a prisoner holds out a gold watch
beats.summary: Lupin says prison is a rest cure and promises to smoke a cigar at Ganimard's house on Wednesday; he returns Ganimard's watch and shows the judge's gold watch.

beats.scene: A prisoner examines a gold-banded cigar as his cell door opens
beats.summary: In The Escape of Arsène Lupin, the prisoner is studying a fine gold-banded cigar after lunch when the guard comes for his exercise hour; he drops it in the drawer and goes out cheerfully.

beats.scene: Two inspectors search a bare prison cell while the prisoner is outside
beats.summary: Inspectors Dieuzy and Folenfant search his cell, because the Grand Journal has printed a letter in his handwriting, so he must be in touch with accomplices.

beats.scene: A police chief lifts books and clippings from a prison table drawer
beats.summary: They find nothing until the guard points to the table drawer; Dudouis lists the clippings, tobacco box, pipe and two annotated books, Carlyle's Hero-Worship and a Manual of Epictetus.

beats.scene: A police chief draws a thin roll of paper from inside a cigar
beats.summary: Dudouis squeezes the cigar by his ear and it cracks; inside is a tiny roll in a woman's writing about a basket, a plate that goes down, and H-P waiting from twelve to sixteen.

beats.scene: A police chief explains a coded note to two inspectors
beats.summary: Dudouis decodes it: twelve to sixteen means noon to four, and H-P means horsepower, an automobile; the letter will be photographed and put back so that Lupin suspects nothing.

beats.scene: A police chief unscrews the handle of a table knife and finds a paper
beats.summary: That evening the knife's handle unscrews to reveal Lupin's reply: he trusts his friend, H-P is to follow at a distance every day, and he will go ahead; Dudouis is delighted.

beats.scene: A judge and a lawyer face a smiling prisoner in an office
beats.summary: Judge Bouvier gets nothing from Lupin until he admits every robbery, and ten times more; each noon Lupin is taken by prison van to the Dépôt.

beats.scene: A prison van with small compartments rolls across a bridge in Paris
beats.summary: One afternoon Lupin is taken back alone in the van, the salad basket with its small compartments; he presses the metal plate with his right foot and it moves.

beats.scene: A man leaps from a prison van while a fallen horse blocks the street
beats.summary: At the corner of Saint-Germain a fallen horse blocks the traffic; Lupin jumps down, walks to a café terrace and tells the owner he is Lupin and has forgotten his wallet.

beats.scene: A man in a hat faces a prison sentinel at a great iron gate
beats.summary: Lupin strolls to the Santé and asks to regain his cell; to the keeper he says that twenty agents were following the van and that when he wishes to escape he will need no help.

beats.scene: A judge listens as a prisoner leans forward and speaks firmly
beats.summary: The Echo de France prints a full account of the attempt, even the messages; Lupin tells Judge Bouvier it was only the first step of his plan and that he will not be present at his trial.

beats.scene: A prisoner lies on a narrow bed with his face to the wall
beats.summary: Lupin is moved to another cell and lies for two months facing the wall; the public waits for his escape, and the day before the trial a stranger leaves a card: Arsène Lupin always keeps his promises.

beats.scene: A dark rainy day in a crowded courtroom as a shabby prisoner enters
beats.summary: A great crowd fills the court; the prisoner shambles in with a stupid look, and when asked his name says in a thick voice that he is Baudru, Désiré.

beats.scene: A judge reads from his notes while a thin bearded prisoner sways
beats.summary: The judge reviews what is known of Lupin's past and calls the name a new alias; the thin prisoner stands stooped and says only the same name.

beats.scene: A famous detective peers closely at a prisoner in a crowded court
beats.summary: Ganimard, nervous, asks to see the prisoner at close range and swears on oath that he is not Arsène Lupin, because of his alcoholic eyes.

beats.scene: Guards and a gaoler peer at a puzzled man in a crowded court
beats.summary: The court laughs; the gaoler sees only a slight likeness, a guard says the man has lain in cell twenty-four for two months, and the prisoner says he was seized outside the Dépôt.

beats.scene: A poor man steps out of a prison gate on a foggy morning
beats.summary: The records show that Baudru left the Dépôt at the same hour as Lupin; he is freed, Ganimard has him followed, and at a waiting-room with two exits Ganimard loses his assistants.

beats.scene: A man on a park bench laughs while a detective seizes his collar
beats.summary: Ganimard follows Baudru to the Bois de Boulogne and sits beside him on a bench; the man bursts into Lupin's laugh, and the dull face changes before his eyes.

beats.scene: Two men sit on a park bench, one rubbing a stiff arm
beats.summary: Ganimard tries to strangle him, but Lupin disables his arm with a Japanese blow; Lupin explains how chemicals, diet and drops in the eyes slowly turned him into Baudru.

beats.scene: A man in a dark coat walks away from a park bench at dusk
beats.summary: Lupin says Baudru was a real man he had copied, that the van, cigar and letters were a bluff, and that he will keep the mistake secret; he leaves to dine with the British Ambassador.

beats.scene: A gentleman with an overcoat stands beside a railway carriage in Paris
beats.summary: In The Mysterious Traveller, a gentleman sends his automobile to Rouen and goes by train; at Paris seven men crowd into his compartment, five of them smoking, and he moves to the next one.

beats.scene: A nervous lady speaks to her husband at a train window
beats.summary: The lady in the next compartment is annoyed, but her husband studies the traveller and reassures her with a smile; he says he has an important appointment, kisses her and leaves, and the train starts.

beats.scene: A well-dressed man bursts into a train compartment as the train starts
beats.summary: A man rushes into the compartment despite the guards; the lady cries out and falls on the seat, but he is elegant, with a refined face the traveller seems to remember.

beats.scene: A frightened lady whispers to a gentleman while a stranger sits nearby
beats.summary: The lady grows pale and slowly draws her travelling bag towards her; asked if she is ill, she whispers that Arsène Lupin is on the train.

beats.scene: A man speaks calmly to a nervous lady in a railway carriage
beats.summary: He reminds her that Lupin was sentenced the day before to twenty years and is said to be in Turkey, but she insists: her husband directs the prison service and the stationmaster warned them.

beats.scene: A lady and a gentleman talk anxiously while a stranger pulls his hat down
beats.summary: Lupin vanished in the station and may have taken the express or leaped into this train; she is sure he will escape the police at Rouen, and the traveller wishes him a good journey.

beats.scene: A traveller sleeps with a newspaper on his knee while a lady watches him
beats.summary: He reads of Lupin's trial but is tired; the lady protests that sleep would be imprudent, he promises not to, then falls asleep and dreams that Lupin leaps on his chest.

beats.scene: A man kneels on another man's chest in a train and ties his wrists
beats.summary: He wakes with a cry: the stranger kneels on his chest and grips his throat, and is bound and gagged with ease; he reflects that he, Arsène Lupin, has been tied up like a novice.

beats.scene: A thief empties a lady's bag while she holds out her rings
beats.summary: The thief takes the traveller's purse and wallet, with twelve thousand francs and papers, then the lady's jewels; she hands him her rings to save him trouble and faints.

beats.scene: A bound man lies on a train seat as the train rushes on
beats.summary: The traveller cares less for the money than for the ending: he is known to his friends as Guillaume Berlat, his presence was noticed, and at Rouen the police will find him tied like a parcel.

beats.scene: A man in an overcoat steps out of a moving train in a tunnel
beats.summary: The thief checks the time-table, takes the lady's umbrella and the traveller's overcoat in the rain, crosses the Seine, opens the door in a tunnel where the train slows, and leaps out.

beats.scene: A lady unties a gag from a bound man in a railway carriage
beats.summary: The lady wakes, mourns her jewels, and removes the traveller's gag but is told not to untie him; he tells her to describe the thief to the police and to give his name as Guillaume Berlat.

beats.scene: A woman waves and shouts on a station platform beside a police commissary
beats.summary: At Rouen Madame Renaud cries that Lupin has attacked them and robbed her; her brother Georges Ardelle is there, and the commissary confirms the gray overcoat with the black velvet collar.

beats.scene: Policemen free a bound man while a lady points at the railway carriage
beats.summary: The traveller, his lips bloody from the gag, tells the commissary it was Lupin and that he can help; he wants to reach his automobile, but two policemen have already gone to the tunnel on bicycles.

beats.scene: A man points at a railway time-table while a commissary listens in surprise
beats.summary: He says that the thief is at Darnétal and will take the train to Amiens at ten fifty, because he consulted the time-table; Madame Renaud insists that he be heard, so two policemen go with him.

beats.scene: A fast automobile speeds along a boulevard with two policemen in the back
beats.summary: In his fast Moreau-Lepton the traveller feels proud, going in search of himself; at Darnétal they arrive three minutes after the train and learn that a man in a gray overcoat has gone to Amiens.

beats.scene: A car races beside an express train on a country road
beats.summary: The car races the Northern Express side by side for the twenty-three kilometres to Montérolier-Buchy and wins by twenty lengths, but the thief has leaped off and Massol chases him into a grove.

beats.scene: A man creeps through a thick wood toward a ruined hut
beats.summary: He posts Massol on the left and Delivet on the right, promising a pistol shot if he needs them, then follows footprints through the wet grass to a ruined hut and sees the thief.

beats.scene: A man holds another down on the floor of a ruined hut
beats.summary: In two bounds he seizes the thief before he can fire, offers to spare him the police, and when the man draws a knife stuns him; he recovers his papers and learns the name Pierre Onfrey.

beats.scene: A man leaves an envelope and a lady's handbag on a hovel floor
beats.summary: He leaves two banknotes and a card of thanks for the policemen and Madame Renaud's emptied handbag, fires a shot to call them, and drives away; the newspapers report how Lupin arrested Onfrey.

beats.scene: A glittering diamond necklace lies in an old red leather case
beats.summary: In The Queen's Necklace, the Countess de Dreux-Soubise wears the famous necklace made for Madame Du Barry, which Cardinal de Rohan meant for Marie-Antoinette and Jeanne de la Motte pulled to pieces in 1785.

beats.scene: A nobleman examines a mounting and a few diamonds in a jeweller's shop
beats.summary: Only the mounting is genuine: Villette kept it and sold it to Gaston de Dreux-Soubise, who bought back a few diamonds from an English jeweller and added lesser stones.

beats.scene: A count carries a red leather case out of a bank
beats.summary: The present count loves the necklace like his ancestors' home; he keeps it in a bank box and fetches it himself when his wife wishes to wear it.

beats.scene: A countess in a ball gown wears a glittering necklace beside a king
beats.summary: At the reception at the Palais de Castille, given for King Christian, the countess has a great success; the diamonds shine like flames and the king praises her grace.

beats.scene: A count places a red leather case on a high shelf among hat-boxes
beats.summary: At home the count puts the necklace in its red case, hides it on a high shelf in the little cabinet at the foot of their bed and bolts their chamber door.

beats.scene: A man and a woman search a small dark cabinet among linen
beats.summary: Next morning the count goes to the stables, then finds the necklace gone from the shelf; they search everything in vain, and the countess calls the commissary Valorbe.

beats.scene: A police commissary examines a narrow window above a small dark courtyard
beats.summary: The door was bolted and the cabinet's only window, onto a small court, is fastened; nobody knew the hiding place, unless perhaps Henriette.

beats.scene: A poor woman sews beside her small son who is reading
beats.summary: Henriette, a school friend of the countess, lives with her son Raoul in a poor room in the house; she laughs at the suspicion but admits that she always knew where the necklace was kept.

beats.scene: A judge examines a bolt and a small window in an old house
beats.summary: The examining judge questions the servants, tests the bolt and the window and searches the court, and Henriette's past is studied; after a week he calls it a double mystery.

beats.scene: A worried count and countess sit among bills and papers
beats.summary: After four months the judge privately believes the hard-pressed couple have sold the necklace and closes the inquiry; the loss hurts their credit, and only two legacies save them from ruin.

beats.scene: A countess sends away a poor seamstress while a small boy clings to her
beats.summary: The countess turns her spite on Henriette, accuses her openly and dismisses her; months later she receives a letter of thanks from Henriette, who has been sent two thousand francs by post.

beats.scene: A poor woman reads a letter holding banknotes by candlelight
beats.summary: The same letter and sum arrive every year, doubled in the fifth and sixth years, signed with false names, until Henriette dies after six years and the mystery remains.

beats.scene: Elegant dinner guests sit around a table after the meal
beats.summary: Years later the count gives a dinner for several guests, among them the Chevalier Floriani, whom he met in Sicily, and the Marquis de Rouzières teases him about the Queen's Necklace.

beats.scene: A calm gentleman speaks to a circle of listening dinner guests
beats.summary: Floriani says he has no opinion, but after the count tells the story he calls the problem simple: the thief came through the window, using a bridge between the kitchen balcony and the ledge.

beats.scene: A count rushes from a dining room while guests sit in tense silence
beats.summary: Floriani says the small transom was opened with a hooked poker through a hole in the putty; the count denies it, rushes out, and returns pale: the hole is exactly there.

beats.scene: A gentleman explains with gestures while a count listens in shock
beats.summary: The transom is too small for a man, so the thief was a child, Henriette's son Raoul, who used the kitchen shelves for a bridge; the count finds them unnailed and the poker still there.

beats.scene: A countess points angrily at a quiet gentleman across a dinner table
beats.summary: The countess blames the mother; Floriani says she slept, and that the boy, free to go out, could sell one diamond at a time in another city and have the money sent from Paris.

beats.scene: Dinner guests stare in alarm at a calm gentleman
beats.summary: Floriani pictures the sick mother and the boy selling the stones to save her, and the man who returns to the house where she was accused; everyone understands that he is Henriette's son.

beats.scene: A count smiles stiffly at a guest who laughs quietly
beats.summary: The count hides his anger and jokes about the boy's brilliant start at six; Floriani says it cost him no trouble and tells the countess most of the diamonds were false.

beats.scene: A red leather case with a cardinal's arms lies open on a table
beats.summary: The countess says that the necklace still belongs to the house of Dreux-Soubise; Floriani promises to tell him, and four days later the red case is on her table and the newspapers name Lupin.

beats.scene: Two friends walk home along a dark street at night
beats.summary: In The Seven of Hearts, a young journalist explains how he met Lupin, by chance, on the night of 22 June after a dinner of crime stories; his friend Jean Daspry walks him home to Neuilly.

beats.scene: A man unlocks the door of a dark isolated house at night
beats.summary: Daspry asks if he is afraid of the lonely house; inside, the journalist remembers that his servant Antoine is away, bolts his bedroom door and puts his revolver beside the bed.

beats.scene: A man in bed holds a letter closed with five red seals
beats.summary: Instead of the paper-knife in his book he finds an envelope with five red seals, marked Urgent: whatever he hears, he must not move or cry out, or he is doomed.

beats.scene: A man lies rigid in bed watching a curtain move in a dark room
beats.summary: He cannot even blow out the candle; he hears noises from the library, sees a curtain move and a human form behind it, and understands that a guard is watching him.

beats.scene: A man lies awake sweating in bed while noises echo through a dark house
beats.summary: A terrific noise shakes the house, then hammering; he does not move, from weakness and discretion, and spends the night in torture until a milk wagon passes.

beats.scene: A man in a nightshirt fires a revolver at a window curtain at dawn
beats.summary: At daylight he fires at the curtain; the bullet breaks the glass but hits no one, because there was no man: he was hypnotised by a fold of the curtain.

beats.scene: A man crouches in a library lifting a rug to find a playing card
beats.summary: In the library everything is in its place, with no clue and no footprint; under a small Persian rug he finds a seven of hearts with a small round hole in each heart.

beats.scene: A large library with a mosaic floor and a mosaic king holding a sword
beats.summary: He studies the library, with its mosaic floor and walls, a mosaic emperor with a crown and sword, and a high window; no ladder marks; he writes an article for the Gil Blas, which people take for fiction.

beats.scene: A dark-haired man in a frayed suit talks to a young journalist
beats.summary: A few mornings later a rough man of about forty says he read the article and may have information, but first he must be alone in the library for three minutes.

beats.scene: A man lies on a library floor beside a smoking revolver
beats.summary: He waits downstairs watching the minutes; a pistol shot sounds, and he finds the man dead on the floor, with a revolver near and another pierced seven of hearts two feet away.

beats.scene: A police chief and a doctor kneel in a library beside a body
beats.summary: Dudouis and the police find no papers, no name, no initials on the dead man; as the body is lifted a crumpled card falls from his hand: Georges Andermatt, 37 rue de Berry.

beats.scene: A banker in a fur coat looks at a covered body
beats.summary: Andermatt, a rich banker and founder of the Metal Exchange, is telephoned by Dudouis, comes at once, and names the dead man as Etienne Varin, whom he knows only by sight, and mentions his brother Alfred.

beats.scene: Newspaper readers argue over a card in a busy café
beats.summary: The banker cannot explain his card; the inquiry shows the Varin brothers were Swiss, lived under various names and knew a band of thieves, and nobody knows where they went; Daspry grows ever more interested.

beats.scene: Two men read a newspaper about a new submarine named Seven-of-Hearts
beats.summary: Daspry shows a news item: a new submarine, to be tried in secret before the former Emperor, is called the Seven-of-Hearts; later the plans are said to be by French engineers who first approached the British Admiralty.

beats.scene: A newspaper column signed Salvator lies on a table beside a lamp
beats.summary: The Echo de France article says that ten years ago the engineer Louis Lacombe rented this very house, was introduced by the Varin brothers to Andermatt, dined at his house one night, and vanished.

beats.scene: A newspaper headline threatens a banker while reporters crowd his door
beats.summary: Salvator says the plans are with the Varin brothers and were sold to a foreign power, but the final document is missing; he accuses Andermatt of silence and spies, and threatens him.

beats.scene: A veiled lady enters a dining room where two men sit among newspapers
beats.summary: That evening a lady in a thick veil enters; she raises it and says she is Madame Andermatt, come hoping for information about the affair.

beats.scene: A veiled lady speaks sadly to two men while a lamp burns
beats.summary: She says Lacombe left her husband's house with a satchel of papers that the Varins later held, with letters she wrote him, and they threatened to publish them, so that her husband feared a scandal.

beats.scene: A lady and two men talk anxiously around a table in a library
beats.summary: She thinks the letters are hidden in this house, in one of Lacombe's safes, opened by her husband on 22 June; Daspry says Salvator was the visitor and tells her to write to him.

beats.scene: A short note signed S lies beside a pierced playing card
beats.summary: Two days later she sends them Salvator's reply: he has not found the letters but will get them; the handwriting matches the note in the writer's book, but the two cards and the submarine's name remain puzzling.

beats.scene: A man with a pickaxe examines the brick walls and roof of a house
beats.summary: Daspry searches the house for the hiding-place, from the foundations to the slates of the roof, then arrives with a pickaxe and a spade and leads the writer to a small mound in the vacant lots.

beats.scene: Two men dig in a vacant lot and find an iron plate
beats.summary: They dig for an hour; the pickaxe unearths old bones, and the writer finds an iron plate the size of a playing card with seven pierced red spots, and goes home feverish for two days.

beats.scene: A man reads a letter while his friend taps the library wall
beats.summary: Daspry searches the library daily; on the third day Salvator writes asking for the use of the house that evening from nine to eleven so that two adversaries can meet.

beats.scene: Two men sit in a lamplit room with the garden gate left unlocked
beats.summary: The writer will not betray Salvator's trust but decides to stay and watch; he sends his servant to the theatre, leaves the gate unlocked, and Daspry agrees to stay too.

beats.scene: A veiled lady whispers urgently to two men beside a door
beats.summary: Madame Andermatt arrives early: her husband is coming to an appointment to exchange the Lacombe papers for the letters; the three hide behind the velvet curtain of the chimney.

beats.scene: A bearded man climbs a chair to study a mosaic king
beats.summary: Alfred Varin enters, slouching and bearded like his brother, and feels the outline of the mosaic king; Andermatt arrives, and each says the other's letter summoned him.

beats.scene: A banker blocks a door while a bearded man tries to leave
beats.summary: Varin, suspecting a trap, tries to go home, but Andermatt bars the way and says it is a good time to speak.

beats.scene: Two men face each other angrily in a library at night
beats.summary: Andermatt asks what Varin did with Lacombe, whom he saw leave with two men slinking in the shadows; Varin says the papers were found on the table; each accuses the other of wanting the letters.

beats.scene: A man points a revolver at a banker while another man fires
beats.summary: Varin draws a revolver and demands yes or no; Daspry shoots it from his hand, steps between the men and says that hearts are trumps and he plays the seven, holding up the iron plate.

beats.scene: A bearded man stares in terror at an iron plate with red spots
beats.summary: Varin, livid and hypnotised, asks who he is; Daspry demands the papers sold to Major von Lieben, and after bargaining they agree on ten thousand francs.

beats.scene: A banker signs a check while a man holds out a checkbook
beats.summary: Daspry tells the banker to sign a check for ten thousand francs and hands him his own checkbook, to his astonishment; then he asks Varin for the letters.

beats.scene: A man with an awl presses a mosaic king's sword as a safe opens
beats.summary: Varin claims the letters are not in the hiding-place; Daspry fits the iron plate on the mosaic king's sword, presses seven stones with an awl and opens a large steel safe, which is empty.

beats.scene: A bearded man reaches into a small safe hidden inside a larger one
beats.summary: Varin says his brother took them; Daspry insists, and when the banker agrees to pay, Varin uses the plate again, and a smaller safe in the door reveals a sealed packet of letters.

beats.scene: A banker takes a sealed packet while a lady listens behind a curtain
beats.summary: The exchange is made; Daspry pockets the document and the checks and hands the letters to Andermatt, who hesitates and takes them; Madame Andermatt moans, her hand cold.

beats.scene: A man puts papers in his pocket and holds a bearded man's arm
beats.summary: Daspry pockets Varin's papers and refuses to pay for stolen goods; when Varin rages, he speaks of the little mound in the vacant lot where Lacombe's plate and body were buried, and Varin gives up.

beats.scene: A bearded man asks a question as another man smiles and names himself
beats.summary: Varin asks whether a casket was in the safe on 22 June; Daspry says yes, with diamonds and pearls, and he took it; Varin sees why his brother died, and asks his name: Arsène Lupin.

beats.scene: A lady revives with smelling salts while a man hands her a packet
beats.summary: Madame Andermatt faints, thinking Daspry gave her real letters to her husband; Daspry says the banker has careful copies written by him and gives her the genuine ones.

beats.scene: A man in a dark coat speaks lightly to a startled writer
beats.summary: Madame Andermatt thanks him as she would a gentleman; the writer is stunned that his club friend is Arsène Lupin, who says to say farewell to Jean Daspry, who will go to Morocco.

beats.scene: A man points at a mosaic king while explaining to a friend
beats.summary: Lupin says he found the small safe only the day before; the mosaic emperor is the king of hearts, and turning the plate upside down changes the pattern; on 22 June he frightened the writer with crime stories.

beats.scene: A newspaper announces a gift of a submarine while two men smile
beats.summary: Lupin announces that he has given Lacombe's papers to the Minister of Marine and subscribed twenty thousand francs, from the banker's checks; so the writer became his historian.

beats.scene: A man struggles with a stranger on a dark road beside a gravel pile
beats.summary: In Madame Imbert's Safe, a man walking home at three in the morning is followed, attacked and thrown on a heap of gravel; a stranger with a cane beats off the attacker and asks if he is hurt.

beats.scene: A shaken gentleman in a carriage takes a card from his rescuer
beats.summary: The rescuer takes him home to the avenue de la Grande-Armée; Ludovic Imbert thanks him, invites him to breakfast, and receives a card: Arsène Lupin, a name just invented.

beats.scene: A shabbily dressed young man talks quietly to a friend on a tram
beats.summary: Lupin dresses in shabby clothes; on a tram his accomplice, the lodger who played the attacker, asks if it is fixed; Lupin says he has studied the Imberts for six months and hopes for millions.

beats.scene: A plump woman and a small gentleman greet a poor young man at breakfast
beats.summary: Madame Gervaise Imbert, short, plump and talkative, treats him as an old friend and tells him about the hundred millions of the old Brawford, which an injunction forbids her to touch.

beats.scene: A young man sits at a desk in a room above a safe
beats.summary: The Imberts make him private secretary for a hundred francs a month, with a room directly above Ludovic's office; the work is nothing, and he secretly visits the office to study the safe.

beats.scene: A young man lies on a floor looking through a small lead pipe
beats.summary: He drills a lead pipe through the floor to watch the safe, but cannot learn the combination; one day he sees them leave it open, but they return, and Ludovic sells annuities for forty-six thousand francs.

beats.scene: Servants whisper in a hall while a poor secretary passes by
beats.summary: The servants never learn his name and the Imberts treat him as an eccentric barbarian; newspapers accuse the Imberts of swindling, and on the sixth evening he learns they will inventory the safe.

beats.scene: A man slides down a rope outside a lit office window at midnight
beats.summary: After dinner the Imberts check the safe; at midnight Lupin climbs down a knotted rope to the office window he left unbolted, and Madame Imbert goes to bed.

beats.scene: A man in the dark binds another man with a curtain beside a safe
beats.summary: Ludovic rises to close the window; Lupin gently stuns him, binds him, empties the safe into a carriage and removes all traces; next morning the Imberts have vanished.

beats.scene: An angry man laughs and waves his arms while telling a story
beats.summary: Later Lupin tells the sequel: the bonds were counterfeit, he had been used to play the invisible Brawford, and Gervaise owed him fifteen hundred francs, his savings; it was the first time he was played for a fool.

beats.scene: A man climbs a dark staircase in a Paris apartment building at night
beats.summary: In The Black Pearl, at three in the morning a visitor asks the concierge of number nine, avenue Hoche, for Doctor Harel, but climbs to the fifth floor, where one of his two keys fits a lock.

beats.scene: A man in felt slippers studies a plan in a dark hallway
beats.summary: He wedges a piece of iron in the street door so it cannot lock, slips back in, puts his hat and coat on a chair, covers his shoes with felt slippers and unfolds a plan of the apartment.

beats.scene: A man counts his steps along a dark corridor toward a glass door
beats.summary: He counts metres along the corridor to the wardrobe-closet door, which he expected to be bolted, and finds it open; he spends half an hour silently opening the second door, of glass, to the countess's bedroom.

beats.scene: A man crawls across a bedroom carpet in the dark
beats.summary: He creeps round the reclining chair toward the table where the pearl is hidden in a box of letter-paper; his hand finds an overturned candlestick and a clock, and then a cold human face.

beats.scene: A thief with a lantern kneels beside a still figure in a dark bedroom
beats.summary: With his lantern he sees that the countess is dead and that there has been a struggle; the clock shows twenty past eleven; the letter-paper box is in place, but the jewel case in it is empty.

beats.scene: A man sits in an armchair with his head in his hands
beats.summary: He admits that with the countess dead and the pearl gone, the situation is unpleasant, and that anyone but Lupin would run; he decides to act like the commissary, but first he must clear his muddled brain.

beats.scene: A beautiful singer in an old opera costume wears a black pearl
beats.summary: The dead woman was Léotine Zalti, once-famous singer and widow of the Count d'Andillot; her wealth was lost, and only the black pearl, the gift of an emperor, remained.

beats.scene: A servant in livery is led away between two policemen
beats.summary: Two days later the papers report the arrest of Victor Danègre, the countess's servant: spots on his waistcoat sleeve, a missing button found by the bed; but one point is obscure, how he left the locked apartment.

beats.scene: A young woman reads a letter while a detective argues with a judge
beats.summary: The inquiry finds Danègre a dangerous criminal; the heiress, Mademoiselle de Sinclèves, says a letter about the hiding-place vanished; the concierge's visitor is unexplained; Ganimard blames Lupin, but the judge doubts it.

beats.scene: A lawyer argues to a jury while a servant in livery sits pale
beats.summary: The judge, swayed by Danègre's bad record, closes the inquiry; at the slow trial his lawyer asks who made the key, who saw the knife and whether the clock was turned, and Danègre is acquitted.

beats.scene: A thin pale man in a small attic room looks nervously at the door
beats.summary: Danègre leaves prison weak and afraid, takes the false name Anatole Dufour, rents a room in Montmartre and lives on odd jobs; three times he is recognised and dismissed, and he fears detectives.

beats.scene: A pale man at a restaurant table raises a glass opposite a calm stranger
beats.summary: A stranger sits at his table and drinks to Victor Danègre; he gives his card, Grimaudan, ex-inspector, and says the heiress sent him to recover the black pearl.

beats.scene: A man lays a copied key on a restaurant table
beats.summary: Danègre says the jury acquitted him, but Grimaudan tells him to save his fine phrases: three weeks before the crime he had the cook's key copied by Outard; he shows the key, then the knife from the Bazar de la République.

beats.scene: A pale man bows his head as another man speaks sternly
beats.summary: Grimaudan adds that in the wardrobe-closet Danègre left his thumb mark on the plaster, which the police never looked for; Danègre bows his head and asks what he would get for the pearl: his life.

beats.scene: A man pours two glasses of wine while another holds a letter
beats.summary: The pearl is useless to him and he cannot sell it; he must give it up tonight, within the hour, or Grimaudan will post a letter to the prosecutor; Danègre drinks two glasses and agrees.

beats.scene: Two men walk through a lamplit Paris street toward a park at night
beats.summary: They walk down the rue Lepic to the Parc Monceau; Danègre sinks onto a bench near the house and says the pearl is between two paving stones; he asks for the price of a steerage ticket to America.

beats.scene: A man digs a black pearl from between wet paving stones at night
beats.summary: Danègre says to count from the sewer-hole to the twelfth and thirteenth stones; Grimaudan digs with a pocketknife, finds the pearl about ten centimetres down, and pays two hundred francs.

beats.scene: A newspaper page announces the recovery of a famous black pearl
beats.summary: Next day the Echo de France announces that Arsène Lupin has recovered the pearl from the countess's murderer and will consider propositions from buyers through his agents.

beats.scene: A man in a dark coat tells a story to a friend by lamplight
beats.summary: Lupin tells the writer that the forty minutes in the dead countess's apartment were the most thrilling of his life: he decided a servant must be arrested, left the button, took the knife and key, and used the law to crush him.

beats.scene: A man holds a black pearl in his palm and gazes at it tenderly
beats.summary: Lupin says Danègre is alive, who might have sunk deeper if he had kept the pearl; he takes the pearl from a secret pocket of his wallet and wonders what prince, rajah or millionaire will own it.

beats.scene: Dinner guests laugh around a long table in a castle hall
beats.summary: In Sherlock Holmes Arrives Too Late, at the Château de Thibermesnil the banker Devanne tells his guest Horace Velmont, a painter, that he looks like Lupin; Velmont is vexed and the guests laugh.

beats.scene: Officers and a painter laugh around a candlelit table
beats.summary: An officer says the police have a description of Lupin since his exploit on the Paris-Havre express; Devanne jokes that Velmont's visits are a preamble to a more serious visit one of these nights.

beats.scene: A vast stone hall with tapestries and a huge Renaissance bookcase
beats.summary: In the Hall of the Guards, with its chests, tapestries and an immense bookcase carrying the name Thibermesnil in gold, Devanne tells Velmont that tonight is his last chance.

beats.scene: A banker raises a hand to announce a famous detective's visit
beats.summary: Devanne announces that Sherlock Holmes will be his guest at four tomorrow; Lupin and his band are near, credited with thefts at Montigny, Gruchet and Crasville, but this time there was no warning letter.

beats.scene: A banker points to an empty space between two huge old books
beats.summary: A month earlier a sixteenth-century book, the Chronique de Thibermesnil, vanished, with a sketch of a secret passage into this hall; the next day the other copy in the National Library was carried off.

beats.scene: A banker explains a plan on a table to his guests
beats.summary: The police found no clue, so Devanne asked Holmes, who accepted; the passage ends at a circle marked T and G, the Tour Guillaume, but the secret was lost when Geoffroy was beheaded in the Revolution.

beats.scene: A priest in black shows an old book to men around a table
beats.summary: Father Gélis says two kings of France knew the key: Henry the Fourth, told by Duke Edgard, and Louis the Sixteenth; Sully wrote the sentence: turn one eye on the bee that shakes, the other eye will lead to God.

beats.scene: A painter rises and speaks, his hand on a banker's shoulder
beats.summary: Louis the Sixteenth's paper in the Iron Casket said Thibermesnil 3-4-11; Velmont laughs, thanks Devanne for the missing key and says he must plunder the castle that night, before Holmes arrives.

beats.scene: A castle at night under the moon with one lit window
beats.summary: Devanne drives Velmont to Dieppe, meets the d'Androls and a young lady at the midnight train, and the castle sleeps; at three o'clock something clicks and a ray of light shoots from a column of the bookcase.

beats.scene: A bookcase swings open on a hidden tunnel as men carry out furniture
beats.summary: The bookcase turns on a pivot; Lupin enters with eight men and chooses what to take, and armchairs, tapestries and paintings are pushed into the tunnel; in forty minutes the room is empty.

beats.scene: A man fills a linen bag with watches from a glass cabinet
beats.summary: Lupin sends his men off with the furniture, keeps a motor-cycle, closes the bookcase, erases the footprints and breaks open a glass cabinet of watches, snuff-boxes, rings and miniatures in the gallery.

beats.scene: A candle glows on a stair as a man hides behind a curtain
beats.summary: He hears a sound; a door opens at the top of a stairway, and he hides behind a window curtain as a young woman comes down with a candle and finds the broken cabinet.

beats.scene: A young woman with a candle faces a startled thief in a dim gallery
beats.summary: They stand face to face: it is Miss Nelly, the girl from La Provence who dropped the Kodak into the sea; he realises he looks like a thief caught in the act, blushes, and drops everything into an armchair.

beats.scene: A thief bows to a young woman clutching a candle in a dark hall
beats.summary: She flees to the salon; he follows and promises that tomorrow at three o'clock everything will be returned, the furniture too; she hears footsteps and begs him to go, and he vanishes.

beats.scene: Gendarmes and police search a castle hall while a banker wrings his hands
beats.summary: Devanne thinks that Velmont is Lupin but cannot believe it; the police find no clue, so the goods must have gone by the secret passage; the old Chronique has been put back beside the stolen copy.

beats.scene: A table of officers and ladies at lunch while a painter arrives late
beats.summary: Officers arrive at eleven; Devanne introduces Monsieur and Madame d'Androl and Miss Nelly; Velmont comes at noon, and Devanne says he has robbed the castle; Nelly is agitated, and Velmont escorts her to the table.

beats.scene: A band plays on a terrace as a young woman glances at a clock
beats.summary: Over coffee on the terrace Nelly remembers Lupin's promise; she watches the clock and Velmont, who swings calmly in a rocking chair, and wonders whether he can keep it.

beats.scene: Two army wagons roll into a castle courtyard as a girl watches
beats.summary: Three o'clock strikes; two army wagons bring all the furniture under a sergeant with an order signed Colonel Beauvel, which an officer calls a clever forgery.

beats.scene: A man bows to a proud young woman holding a white rose
beats.summary: On the terrace Velmont asks Nelly if he has kept his promise, recalls the white rose on the Provence, and begs her to look at him as at Bernard; she points to a ruby ring that is Devanne's; he steps aside.

beats.scene: A man picks fallen petals of a white rose from a flower box
beats.summary: She enters the house and he never sees her again; he finds her white rose on the flower box, forgotten or left on purpose, picks up the petals like relics, and decides to think of his safety.

beats.scene: A man walks across fields toward a narrow sunken lane
beats.summary: Lupin leaves through a pine grove, leaps the wall and takes a path across the fields to the station; in a narrow lane he meets a tall, clean-shaven stranger of about fifty with a heavy cane and a satchel.

beats.scene: Two men face each other in a narrow lane, one with a satchel
beats.summary: The stranger asks in a slight English accent the way to the castle; Lupin says they expect Holmes and that he is his warmest admirer; Holmes's keen look makes him feel photographed.

beats.scene: Two men press against a steep bank as mounted gendarmes ride past
beats.summary: Gendarmes ride by and the two men step aside; Lupin wonders if Holmes has recognised him and will seize the chance; Holmes only brushes the dust from his clothes and says thank you, and they part.

beats.scene: Guests stare in disappointment at an ordinary Englishman in a hall
beats.summary: The castle's people are disappointed by the commonplace look of Holmes; he grumbles at official receptions and says that had his visit not been announced the robbery would not have happened that night.

beats.scene: A detective turns to leave as a banker begs him to stay
beats.summary: Holmes is ready to go home, but Devanne begs him to stay; he studies the two books and the sentences, asks whether Velmont had heard them, and says that Velmont and Lupin are the same man.

beats.scene: A detective kneels to study candle spots at the foot of stairs
beats.summary: Holmes finds fresh candle spots at the foot of the gallery stairs, at the top and by the broken cabinet, which explain the return of the goods; he asks for a ladder and a lantern and a car near the ruined chapel.

beats.scene: A banker on a ladder turns a golden letter on a bookcase
beats.summary: Holmes tells Devanne to turn the first I of Thibermesnil, move the B like a bolt and open the last I like a wicket; the whole bookcase pivots, Devanne falls, and the passage is open.

beats.scene: Two men walk down damp stone steps in a tunnel with a lantern
beats.summary: Holmes explains that Louis the Sixteenth, a locksmith, noted 3-4-11, the third, fourth and eleventh letters; with a lantern they go down flights of twelve steps and along a damp passage under the pond.

beats.scene: A ruined chapel where a tomb swings aside and an automobile waits
beats.summary: At the far end Holmes works the three letters and a block of granite swings out: the tomb of Duke Rollo in the ruined chapel; a car is waiting, and the chauffeur says Velmont sent him.

beats.scene: A detective holds a pocket watch in a car beside a laughing banker
beats.summary: Holmes says he met Lupin on the road and let him go, since he creates chances; the car holds a package, Sherlock Holmes, from Arsène Lupin, with his own watch; at the station Holmes vows that they will meet again.

A1A2: The ship La Provence was fast, and the passengers were happy.
A storm came, and a message said that Lupin was on the ship.
Soon everybody on the ship knew that the famous thief was there.
Miss Nelly asked Bernard if he knew anything about the thief.
Bernard loved Nelly, but he thought a quiet young man loved her too.
Bernard took out the list of passengers and looked for names with R.
The first three men were easy to clear, and the last was Rozaine.
He showed his arm, but it was the left one.
Then Lady Jerland ran up and cried that her jewels were gone.
The thief took the jewels in daylight, and everyone said it was Lupin.
That night, under the moon, Bernard told Nelly that he loved her.
Nobody trusted Rozaine, and Nelly would not speak to him.
Rozaine offered ten thousand francs to anyone who found the thief.
Soon the captain's watch was stolen, but it was found again.
Someone tied Rozaine up and took his money, and left a card.
Everyone was afraid, and nobody wanted to be alone.
At the bottom of the ship's steps stood a little old man with an umbrella.
Ganimard let Rozaine go, but he stopped Bernard.
Nelly walked down and let the camera fall into the sea.
“What a pity that I am not an honest man,” he said sadly.
A small old castle stands on a rock in the river Seine.
A rich old baron lived there alone with his beautiful things.
The baron got a letter from Arsène Lupin in prison.
Lupin wrote that he wanted the baron's best paintings and furniture.
The baron was afraid, so he wrote to the police in Rouen.
The baron read that the detective Ganimard was fishing nearby.
The fisherman said that thieves do not warn people first.
The baron paid Ganimard three thousand francs to help him.
That night, Ganimard locked two men in the gallery of the castle.
In the morning, the paintings were gone, and the men were asleep.
Ganimard saw that the two men had been drugged by something.
Many police and newspaper men came, but they found no tunnel.
Ganimard decided to ask Lupin himself in prison.
Lupin welcomed Ganimard as if he were an old friend.
Lupin said he had planned the whole robbery himself.
Lupin said that the owner of the castle must ask him in.

B1B2: In The Arrest of Arsène Lupin, the liner La Provence was fast and her captain was friendly. The passengers soon became friends, as people do when they share a small island in the middle of the sea.

In a violent storm on the second day, the wireless brought a warning: Arsène Lupin was on board, travelling alone in first class. He had fair hair, a wound on his right arm and a name starting with R, but then lightning cut the message off.

Although the secret should have been kept, by evening every passenger had heard of it. Everyone knew Arsène Lupin, the polite thief who robbed only castles and rich houses and wore a new face every day.

Next morning, the rich and beautiful Nelly Underdown said that five days with a thief on board would be unbearable. She was going to join her father in Chicago, and she asked Bernard d'Andrézy, a friend of the captain, what he knew.

Bernard had meant only to flirt with Nelly, but he now loved her, and he feared that a quiet young man was his rival. As they sat in the sun after the storm, he suggested that they could solve the mystery as well as the detective Ganimard.

Bernard reminded Nelly that the thief was fair, travelling alone and called R, and he took the passenger list from his pocket. Only thirteen men in the first class had a name beginning with R, and nine of them were with wives, children or servants.

Nelly knew the Marquis de Raverdan, a passenger was the nephew of Major Rawson, and the Italian Rivolta had a thick black beard. That left Monsieur Rozaine, a quiet man with fair hair, and when Nelly asked why he said nothing, everyone stared at him.

Rozaine, pale and with bloodshot eyes, said that his name, his hair and his solitude made him the very man to arrest. Asked about the wound, he showed his arm, but Bernard saw that it was the left arm and the message had spoken of the right.

At that moment Lady Jerland rushed towards them in great excitement, crying that her jewels and pearls had been stolen. The thief had taken not the largest but the finest stones, and the empty mountings lay on her table.

The theft had happened in daylight, while Lady Jerland was having tea, in a cabin opening on a busy corridor. Everyone was sure it was Lupin, and that evening they were relieved to hear that the captain had arrested Rozaine.

That evening the passengers danced and played games again, and at midnight, under a bright moon, Bernard told Nelly of his love. Next morning, however, Rozaine was free, for his papers were in order and his arms bore no wound.

His enemies said that Lupin could have any papers he wanted, and that nobody else was fair, alone and called R. When Rozaine came boldly towards their group before breakfast, Nelly and Lady Jerland stood up and walked away.

A handwritten notice went round the ship: Rozaine offered ten thousand francs to anyone who found Lupin or the jewels. For two days he questioned everyone, while the captain searched every cabin from one end of the ship to the other.

Bernard showed Nelly his Kodak and said that all the jewels could be hidden in a camera that small. Soon afterwards the captain's watch was stolen, and the next day it turned up in the second officer's collar box.

That night an officer heard groans in a dark corner and found Rozaine tied up, with a scarf round his head. A card pinned to his coat said that Lupin gladly accepted the ten thousand francs, and the stolen pocket-book had held twenty thousand.

Fear spread through the ship, and nobody dared to stay alone in a cabin or in a quiet part of the deck. Nelly, who was easily frightened, stayed close to Bernard for protection, and he secretly thanked Lupin for bringing them together.

When the ship reached New York, Nelly, pale and nervous, leaned on Bernard's arm as the customs men came aboard. At the foot of the gangway stood a small old man with an umbrella, whom Bernard knew to be the detective Ganimard.

Ganimard let the pale Rozaine pass, and Bernard, who was carrying his bags, gave his camera to Nelly. But when they had taken ten steps, Ganimard stopped them and asked, looking him in the eyes, whether he was Arsène Lupin.

Ganimard struck his right arm, where the wound had not healed, and Bernard had to give himself up. Nelly, who had understood everything, carried the camera down the gangway and, pretending to be clumsy, let it fall into the water.

Lupin stood still for a moment, then told Ganimard, to his surprise, that it was a pity he was not an honest man. Later he told the whole story himself, and he added that nobody could describe his face, because he wore a different one each time.

In Arsène Lupin in Prison, tourists on the Seine all notice the castle of Malaquis, built on a rock. Its past is full of sieges and battles, and a legend tells of a secret tunnel that once led to the abbey of Jumièges.

The castle now belonged to Baron Nathan Cahorn, who had made a great fortune on the Bourse and was called Baron Satan. He lived there alone with three old servants, guarding his three Rubens, his two Watteau paintings and his other treasures.

One Thursday in September, the postman brought the baron a registered letter, which was strange, since he never received any. It came from the Prison de la Santé in Paris, and it was signed Arsène Lupin.

Lupin wrote that he liked the baron's Champaigne, his Rubens and his smallest Watteau, as well as some furniture, tapestries and jewels. He wanted them sent to Batignolles station within eight days, or he would fetch them himself on the night of the twenty-seventh.

The baron knew that Lupin was in prison, but the letter showed an exact knowledge of things that no stranger had ever seen. He wrote to the prosecutor at Rouen, who replied that Lupin was closely guarded and that an expert said the writing was not his.

Two days later the baron read in a local newspaper that the famous detective Ganimard was spending a holiday at Caudebec, six kilometres away. He hurried there, and the editor of the paper pointed out a little man in a straw hat, fishing on the quay.

The fisherman listened without moving, his eyes on his rod, and then said that thieves never warn the people they mean to rob. Nobody ever escaped from the Santé, he added, so the baron should go home and sleep, and stop frightening the fish.

On the twenty-sixth a telegram came: there were no goods at Batignolles, and everything must be ready for tomorrow night. In terror the baron ran to Caudebec and offered three thousand francs, and Ganimard agreed to come with two of his men.

That night Ganimard arrived with two strong assistants, barred every door and window, and locked the men in the central gallery. He and the baron waited in a small room in the wall, and Ganimard lay on three chairs, smoked his pipe and slept.

At dawn the castle was calm, and the baron, delighted, climbed the stairs behind Ganimard. In the gallery the two assistants were asleep on their chairs, and the walls were bare except for nails and cords.

Ganimard stood still, because the windows were closed, the locks were whole and nothing in the room had been broken. He could not wake his assistants, and he decided that they had been drugged, perhaps by the water in the carafe.

Soon the castle was full of gendarmes, judges, reporters and curious visitors, and the newspapers printed Lupin's letter. The police searched the walls, the cellars and the rock for a secret tunnel, but they found nothing.

Ganimard told his chief that it was useless to search the castle, because the solution lay with Arsène Lupin himself. Lupin did not use old-fashioned tricks, he said, and he asked permission to spend an hour with him in his cell.

Lupin jumped up from his bed and welcomed Ganimard like an old friend, apologising for the hard stool and the lack of beer. He complained about the spies who searched him ten times a day, then asked what he could do for his visitor.

Lupin said that he had arranged the whole affair from beginning to end, including the letter and the telegram. He even took the postal receipts from the drawer of his little table, which astonished Ganimard.

The letter, Lupin said, started the whole machine, because a castle that no one can enter must invite the thief itself. The prosecutor would laugh, since Lupin was in prison, and the frightened baron would ask the first detective he heard of for help.

Lupin had sent a friend to Caudebec, where the editor announced him as the famous detective, and the baron swallowed the bait. The false detective took the baron's money and called two men of the band, who lowered the treasures into a launch.

Lupin said that the affair was almost settled, since the baron had probably paid already to recover his treasures. Ganimard, at his request, broke an egg from the lunch tray and found a small blue telegram inside.

Lupin explained that the hundred thousand balls were francs, and Ganimard admitted that France could not survive a dozen such men. Lupin then said that he would not attend his own trial, for he stayed in prison only as long as it pleased him.

Lupin said that prison was a fine rest cure, and that next Wednesday at four o'clock he would smoke a cigar at Ganimard's house. At the door Lupin returned Ganimard's watch, which had strayed into his pocket, and showed the gold watch of Judge Bouvier.

In The Escape of Arsène Lupin, the prisoner has just finished his meal and is studying a fine cigar with a gold band. The door opens, he drops the cigar in a drawer, and the guard takes him out for his hour of exercise.
As soon as Lupin was gone, Inspectors Dieuzy and Folenfant began to search his cell. The Grand Journal had printed a letter in his handwriting, so he was plainly in touch with friends outside.

They searched everywhere and found nothing, until the guard remembered that Lupin had been closing the drawer. Inside, Monsieur Dudouis found newspaper cuttings, a pipe, and two marked books, one by Carlyle and one by Epictetus.

Dudouis, who knew cigars, squeezed it near his ear, and it cracked, for it hid a thin roll of paper. The woman's letter spoke of a basket, a plate that goes down, and a car that would wait every day from twelve to sixteen.

Dudouis worked it out: twelve to sixteen meant noon to four o'clock, and H-P, for horsepower, meant an automobile. He took it to the judge, and they decided to copy the letter and put it back in a similar cigar.

That evening Dudouis cut up the macaroni and opened the bread, but found nothing. Then the handle of the knife unscrewed, and inside was a note promising that the car would follow at a distance every day.

For months Judge Bouvier had questioned Lupin without success, and the advocate Danval argued with him instead. One day Lupin admitted that he had committed every robbery, and ten times more, but he would explain nothing.
One afternoon the other prisoners had not yet been questioned, so Lupin was taken back alone in the van. In the third compartment on the right he pressed a metal plate with his foot, and it moved.

At a corner a fallen horse stopped the traffic, and Lupin slipped through the plate and jumped to the ground. He sat on a café terrace, drank a beer and told the owner, loudly, that he was Arsène Lupin and had forgotten his wallet.

Lupin walked slowly through the streets to the Santé and told the astonished sentinel that he wished to return to his cell. The keeper pretended to be angry, but Lupin said that twenty agents were following the van and he would not have escaped alive.

Two days later the Echo de France printed a full account of the attempt, including the secret messages and the strange van. Lupin told the judge that this was only the first step of his plan and that he would not be at his own trial.

Lupin was moved to another cell, and for two months he lay on his bed with his face to the wall, seeing nobody. Paris expected him to escape, and the day before the trial a gentleman left a card at a newspaper: Lupin always keeps his promises.

The trial began on a dark, rainy day, and an enormous crowd came to see the famous Arsène Lupin play tricks on the judge. But the prisoner who shuffled in looked dull and heavy, and to the judge's question he muttered, “Baudru, Désiré.”

The judge said that Lupin might have been a magician's helper, a hospital student, a teacher of Japanese wrestling or a racing cyclist. The prisoner stood thin and stooped, with a rough beard, and only repeated the name Baudru, Désiré.

When Ganimard was called, he seemed nervous, and he looked at the prisoner several times with doubt. At last he asked to see the man more closely, and then he swore on his oath that this was not Arsène Lupin.

The court rang with laughter, and when the judge called Monsieur Bouvier and the gaoler, they saw only a slight likeness. A guard said that the man had lain in cell twenty-four for two months, and the man said he had been seized outside the Dépôt.

The records showed that a man named Baudru had left the Dépôt at the same hour on the same day as Lupin. After a month the poor man was freed, and Ganimard and two inspectors followed him, hoping he would lead them to Lupin.

Ganimard followed Baudru by omnibus and tram to the Bois de Boulogne, where the tired man sat on a bench beside a pond. When Ganimard sat down beside him, the man burst into laughter, and Ganimard knew that happy laugh very well.

Ganimard seized him by the throat, but a Japanese blow left his right arm useless, and he almost wept with shame. Lupin explained that diet, special drugs, drops in the eyes and endless practice had slowly turned him into poor Baudru.

Baudru was a real man, Lupin said, and the van, the cigar and the letters were a bluff to make everyone expect his escape. Then he promised to keep Ganimard's mistake secret and hurried away to dine with the British Ambassador.

In The Mysterious Traveller, a gentleman sent his automobile to Rouen by road and went there by train himself. In Paris seven men crowded into his compartment, five of them smoking, so he moved to the next one.

A lady in the next compartment looked annoyed, but her husband studied the traveller and calmed her with a smile. He said that he had an important appointment, kissed her goodbye, and the train started.

Just as the train started, a man ran into the compartment, and the lady cried out in terror and fell back on her seat. He was elegantly dressed and had an intelligent face, and the traveller felt sure that he had seen it somewhere.
The lady grew pale and slowly drew her little travelling bag towards her, watching the stranger with fear. At last she whispered to the traveller that Arsène Lupin was on the train.

The traveller said that Lupin had been sentenced the day before to twenty years of hard labour and was said to be in Turkey. But she said that her husband was a director of the prisons and that a search for Lupin was going on.

Lupin had vanished in the station, so he might have taken the express, or leaped into this train at the last moment. The lady was sure he would escape the police at Rouen, and the traveller politely wished him a good journey.

The traveller read about Lupin's trial in his newspapers, but he was tired, and his eyes began to close. The lady cried out that he must not sleep, but he soon dreamed that Lupin leaped on to his chest.

He woke with a cry of pain and found the stranger kneeling on his chest and holding him by the throat. In a moment he was tied up and gagged, and he realised with grim amusement that he, Arsène Lupin, had been beaten like a beginner.

The thief calmly took the traveller's purse and wallet, with twelve thousand francs and papers, and then the lady's jewels. She held out her rings to save him trouble, and when he looked at her, she fainted.

The traveller did not worry about the money, which he felt sure he would recover with his papers. His worry was Rouen, where the police would find Arsène Lupin tied up like a parcel and ready to be delivered.

Rain began to fall, and the thief, after looking at the time-table, put on the traveller's overcoat and took the lady's umbrella. When the train entered a tunnel and slowed down, he opened the door and leaped out.

The lady woke at once and cried about her jewels, and when he looked at her pleadingly, she removed his gag. He would not be untied, and he told her to describe the thief to the police and to give his name as Guillaume Berlat.

At Rouen she called out that Lupin had robbed her, and gave her name as Madame Renaud, wife of a prison director. The commissary agreed that the thief wore a gray overcoat with a black velvet collar, as she said.

The policemen untied him, and he told the commissary in a weak voice that it was Lupin and that he could help. In the station-master's office he offered his automobile, but the commissary had already sent two men on bicycles to the tunnel.

The traveller said that the thief would take the train to Amiens at ten fifty, because he had looked at the time-table. The commissary admired the deduction, and thanks to Madame Renaud's words, two policemen were sent with him.

The traveller drove his fast Moreau-Lepton out of Rouen with the two policemen behind him, proud to be free and out of danger. They reached Darnétal three minutes after the train, and learned that a man in a gray overcoat had bought a ticket for Amiens.

The car raced beside the Northern Express for a kilometre and won by twenty lengths, but the thief was not in the second-class carriages. A man was seen crossing the track, and they ran after him as far as a thick grove.

He posted the two policemen at the edges of the grove and went in alone, promising a pistol shot if he needed them. He followed footprints in the wet grass to a ruined hut and saw the thief's back through a gap in the wall.

In two bounds he reached the thief and threw him down before he could fire, then offered to protect him if he gave back everything. When the man tried to use a knife, a sharp blow to the neck knocked him out.

He left two banknotes and a card of thanks for the policemen, and Madame Renaud's handbag, with nothing valuable in it. He fired a shot in the air and drove away, and next day the Echo de France said that Lupin had arrested Onfrey.
