In The Queen's Necklace, the Countess de Dreux-Soubise sometimes wore the famous necklace called the Queen's Necklace. It had been made for Madame Du Barry, and the Cardinal de Rohan had wanted to give it to Marie-Antoinette.

Only the mounting was real, because the thieves had scattered the beautiful stones long ago. Gaston de Dreux-Soubise, the Cardinal's nephew, bought the mounting, took back a few diamonds from an English jeweller and added cheaper stones.
The present count was devoted to the necklace, as a man is to the home of his ancestors. He kept it in a box at the Crédit Lyonnais, fetching it himself whenever his wife wished to wear it.

At a reception for King Christian at the Palais de Castille, the countess was a great success. The thousand facets of the diamonds shone like flames on her neck, and the king praised her beauty and grace.

At home the countess handed the necklace to her husband with regret, and he admired it as if he had never seen it. He put it in its red case and hid it on a high shelf among hat-boxes and linen in a small cabinet by their bed.

The next morning the count looked in the cabinet and asked his wife, without surprise, if she had taken the necklace. She had not, and when they had searched every box and pile of linen, they admitted that it was gone.

The count was a light sleeper, and he had bolted the door of their chamber. The cabinet's only window, on a small dark court, was fastened, and nobody knew about the hiding place except, perhaps, Henriette.

Henriette had been the countess's school friend, but her family had cast her out for marrying a poor man. Now a widow, she sewed for the countess and lived with her son Raoul in a poor room in the same house.
The judge questioned the servants, tried the bolt and the window and searched the little court, but he found nothing. He had a double mystery, he said: a door and a window, both closed and fastened.

After four months the judge secretly believed that the count and countess had sold the necklace, and he closed the inquiry. Their credit fell, and they would have been ruined if two legacies from distant relatives had not saved them.

The countess took out her anger on her school friend, accused her openly and dismissed her. Months later Henriette wrote to thank the countess for two thousand francs that had come by post, but the countess had sent nothing.

A similar letter with the same sum came every year for six years, and in the last two years the amount was doubled. The senders used false names and false addresses, and when Henriette died the mystery was still unsolved.

Many years later, the count gave a dinner for several guests, among them the Chevalier Floriani, whom he had met in Sicily. When the talk turned to famous crimes, the Marquis de Rouzières teased the count by mentioning his lost necklace.

The Chevalier said that he knew little about the affair, but he listened to the count's story and asked a few questions. Then he said that the problem was simple: the door was bolted, so the thief must have used the window.

Floriani said that the thief had opened the small upper window with a hooked poker, through a hole beside the glass. The count laughed and said there was no hole, but he rushed out to look and came back pale, for it was exactly there.

Floriani said that no man could crawl through such a small opening, so the thief must have been a child, Henriette's son Raoul. The boy had used his mother's kitchen shelves as a bridge, and the count found them unnailed, with the poker still there.

The countess cried that Henriette must have forced her son, but Floriani said that the mother was asleep and knew nothing. The boy, free to come and go, could sell a diamond at a time in a nearby city and have the money sent from Paris.

Floriani described the sick mother, the boy selling stones to save her, and the man who returns to her old home. The count asked who he was, and all the guests understood that the Chevalier was Henriette's son.

The count chose not to make a scandal and joked that the boy had made a brilliant start at six years old. Floriani told the countess that most of the diamonds were false, but she said proudly that it had still been the Queen's Necklace.

The proud countess told the chevalier that the necklace still belonged to her family, even without its stones. Four days later she found the red case on her table, and the newspapers said that Lupin had returned it.

In The Seven of Hearts, a young journalist explains how he met Lupin, by pure chance, on the night of 22 June. After a dinner full of crime stories, he walked home to Neuilly with his friend Jean Daspry.

Daspry asked if he was afraid to live in such a lonely house, and he laughed, though the stories had made him uneasy. Inside, he remembered that his servant Antoine was away, so he bolted his door and put his revolver by the bed.
In his book, instead of the paper-knife, he found an envelope with five red seals, marked Urgent. The letter said that whatever he heard, he must not move or cry out, or he was doomed.
He did not even blow out the candle, but obeyed the letter. Soon he heard noises from the library, and a curtain moved, and behind it he saw a man watching him.

Then a terrible noise shook the house, followed by hammering and other sounds, as if the intruders felt perfectly safe. All night he lay still, wet with sweat and full of fear, until at last a milk wagon passed in the street.
When daylight came, he reached for his revolver and fired at the place behind the curtain. The bullet broke the glass but hit nobody, because there was no man, only a fold of the curtain.

In the library, to his amazement, nothing was missing, and there was no sign that anyone had been there. Under a small Persian rug he found a playing card, a seven of hearts with a small round hole in each heart.

All day he searched the library, a large room with a floor and walls of coloured mosaic, in which a bearded emperor held a sword. He wrote an account for the Gil Blas, but people thought it was fiction, and only Daspry took it seriously.
A few days later a rough-voiced man of about forty came without giving his name. He had read the article and might know something, but first he must stay alone in the library for three minutes.

The journalist waited downstairs with his watch in his hand, and after two minutes and three quarters he heard a shot. He ran up and found the man lying dead, and two feet from the body lay another seven of hearts.

The police arrived, and the chief, Monsieur Dudouis, found nothing on the dead man to show who he was. Then a crumpled card fell from his left hand, with the words Georges Andermatt, thirty-seven rue de Berry.
Georges Andermatt was a rich Paris banker who lived in princely style. Dudouis telephoned him, and he came at once and named the dead man as Etienne Varin, who had a brother, Alfred.
The banker said that he knew of no reason for the suicide, and he could not explain his card. The police learned that the Varin brothers were Swiss, used many names and knew a band of thieves.

Daspry showed him a news item about a new submarine, soon to be tried in secret, called the Seven-of-Hearts. Two days later another report said that French engineers had drawn its plans after finding no help in France.

An article signed Salvator said that ten years earlier an engineer named Louis Lacombe had rented that very house. He worked there on a submarine, and one night, after dining with the banker Andermatt, he vanished.

Salvator wrote that the Varin brothers had sold Lacombe's plans to a foreign power, but the last and most important document was missing. He demanded that Andermatt explain his silence, and ended with a threat.
That evening, while the writer and Daspry discussed the affair, a lady in a thick veil walked in. She raised the veil, showing sad dark eyes, and said that she was Madame Andermatt.

Daspry questioned her, and she said that Lacombe had left her husband's house with a satchel of papers. The Varin brothers soon held those papers, and also private letters that she had written to Lacombe.

She thought that the letters were hidden in one of Lacombe's safes in this house, opened by her husband on 22 June. Daspry replied that Salvator, not the banker, had been the visitor, and told her to write to him and tell him everything.
Two days later she sent them Salvator's reply: he had not found the letters yet, but he would get them. The writer compared it with the note in his book, and the handwriting was the same.

Daspry searched every part of the house, from the foundations to the slates of the roof, looking for the hiding place. One day he brought a pickaxe and a spade and led the writer to the vacant lots nearby.

For an hour they dug under a hot sun, and Daspry's pickaxe uncovered old bones with scraps of clothing. The writer then found an iron plate the size of a playing card, with seven red spots, each with a hole.
The writer was well again by the third day, and that afternoon he received a letter from Salvator. It asked to use his house that evening from nine to eleven, so that two enemies could meet there.

The letter amused him, and he would not betray Salvator's trust, but he was determined to stay and watch. He sent his servant to the theatre and left the garden gate unlocked, and when Daspry arrived he agreed to stay too.
Madame Andermatt arrived twenty minutes early, pale and nervous. At dinner she had read a message meant for her husband, telling him to bring the papers that night for the letters.
Alfred Varin came in first, looking very like his brother, with the same slouching walk and black beard. He glanced at the curtain, then climbed on a chair and felt the shape of the mosaic king.
Each man said that the other's letter had brought him there, and Varin, suspecting a trap, tried to leave. But Andermatt barred the door and said that this was a good time to speak.

Andermatt asked Varin what he had done with Lacombe, since he had seen two men creeping away that night. Varin said that the papers had been on Lacombe's table the next day, and that the banker could prove nothing.
Varin drew a revolver and shouted at Andermatt, but a shot rang out and the revolver fell from his hand. Daspry had fired, and he stepped forward and held up the iron plate with seven red spots.

Varin, white with terror, asked who he was, and Daspry said that he wanted what Varin had brought that night. Varin said he had the originals, and after some bargaining they agreed on ten thousand francs.
Daspry told Andermatt to sign a check, and handed him a checkbook that was in fact the banker's own. Astonished, the banker signed, but Daspry said that there was something more: the letters.

Varin would not open the hiding place, so Daspry climbed on a chair and fitted the iron plate to the king's sword. With an awl he pressed seven stones through the holes, and the whole bust turned, showing a large steel safe, which was empty.

Varin said that his brother must have taken the letters, but Daspry said that there was another hiding place. When Andermatt agreed to pay ten thousand francs for them, Varin closed the safe and used the plate once more.

Daspry took the document and the checks and handed the packet of letters to the banker. Andermatt hesitated as if he feared to touch them, then took them and left, while behind the curtain his wife gave a moan.
Daspry took all the papers, looked at them carefully and put them in his pocket. When Varin asked for his money, Daspry laughed and said that nobody is paid for returning stolen papers.
Varin asked if a small casket had been in the safe on 22 June, and Daspry said yes, and that he had taken it. At last Varin asked his name, and the answer made him stagger: “Arsène Lupin.”
Daspry pushed Varin out of the door, and the writer called that Madame Andermatt was ill. Daspry gave her the true letters and explained that her husband had only copies that he himself had written.
Madame Andermatt thanked him as she would any gentleman, for she had not heard the end of the scene with Varin. The writer was shocked to realise that his club friend Daspry was Arsène Lupin.

Lupin said that the mosaic emperor was an exact copy of the king of hearts on playing cards. When he turned the iron plate upside down, the pattern of the seven spots changed and opened the second safe.

Lupin wrote an article announcing that he had given Lacombe's papers to the Minister of Marine and put his name down for twenty thousand francs. The money came from the banker's checks, since Varin ought to pay for his treachery.

In Madame Imbert's Safe, a man walking home at three in the morning is followed and attacked in the dark. A stranger drives the attacker away with his cane and takes the shaken man home in a carriage.

The man, Ludovic Imbert, thanked his rescuer and invited him to breakfast so that his wife could thank him too. In return, the rescuer gave him a card with the name Arsène Lupin, which he had just invented.

Lupin put on a shabby coat and frayed hat, and on the tram his friend, who had played the attacker, asked what came next. Lupin said that the attack had been staged to win him a place in the Imberts' house, because he wanted the bonds in their safe.

Madame Imbert, a short and talkative woman, welcomed her saviour like an old friend. Over breakfast she told him about the huge fortune of old Brawford, which a legal dispute stopped her from touching.

The Imberts made Lupin their secretary for a hundred francs a month, and gave him a room directly above Ludovic's office. He had almost nothing to do, but he secretly visited the office below to study the huge iron safe.

Lupin made a small hole in the floor and put a lead pipe through it, so that he could watch the safe from above. He spent his days lying on the floor, but he could not learn the numbers of the lock or find the key.
The servants never knew his name and called him monsieur, and Madame Imbert called him a barbarian. When the newspapers accused the Imberts of fraud, Lupin decided that he could not wait any longer.
That night the Imberts worked on their accounts in front of the open safe until midnight. Lupin tied a rope to his balcony, climbed down to the office window and pushed it gently open.

When Imbert got up to close the window, Lupin gently stunned him, wrapped the curtain round his head and bound him. He emptied the safe into a carriage waiting in the street, and next morning the Imberts had vanished.

Later Lupin told the sequel in a rage: the bonds were counterfeit, every one, and worth nothing at all. The Imberts had used him to play the hidden Brawford, and Gervaise even owed him fifteen hundred francs.

In The Black Pearl, a loud bell wakes the concierge of number nine, avenue Hoche, and a man asks for Doctor Harel. But he climbs past the doctor's door to the fifth floor, where one of his two keys fits a lock.

On his way out he put a piece of iron in the lock so that the door would not close, and slipped back in. Upstairs he put on felt slippers, took a plan of the apartment from his pocket and wondered why more people did not become burglars.

Counting each metre in the dark, he followed the corridor to a door that he had expected to find bolted. The door opened at once, so he spent half an hour on the second door, made of glass, with perfect silence.

He crept over the carpet toward the table by the bed, where the pearl lay hidden in a box of letter-paper. His hand found an overturned candlestick and a clock on the floor, and then, with a cry, hair and a cold human face.
With his lantern he saw a woman lying on the floor, and he quickly understood that the countess was dead. The clock showed twenty past eleven, and the jewel case in the box was empty.
Lupin told himself that anyone else would run, but that Arsène Lupin had something better to do. He would act like the commissary of police, but first he sat down, because his brain was muddled.

The dead woman was Léotine Zalti, a famous singer who had married the Count d'Andillot. She had once dazzled Paris with her jewels, but of all her fortune only a black pearl remained, the gift of an emperor.
Two days later the newspapers reported the arrest of the servant, Victor Danègre. Stains were found on his waistcoat, and a button from it lay under the countess's bed.

The police learned that Danègre was a dangerous criminal, and the heiress said that a letter describing the pearl's hiding place had vanished. Ganimard blamed Lupin, but the judge laughed, because the clock showed eleven twenty and the visitor had come at three.
The judge, who disliked Danègre's past, closed the inquiry, and the trial was slow and dull. His lawyer said that nobody had seen a key or a knife, and the jury set Danègre free.

Danègre left prison weak and frightened, took the false name Anatole Dufour and rented a room in Montmartre. He did odd jobs, but three times he was recognised and sacked, and he feared that detectives followed him.

In a restaurant one evening a stranger sat at his table and drank to the health of Victor Danègre. He gave his card, Grimaudan, ex-inspector, and said that the heiress had sent him to recover the black pearl.
Danègre said that twelve jurors had found him innocent, but Grimaudan told him to stop the fine phrases. He said that Danègre had copied the cook's key and bought a knife, and he showed him both.

Grimaudan added that a thumb mark on the closet wall would identify him, though the police had never looked for it. Beaten, Danègre asked what he would get for the pearl, and Grimaudan answered that he would get his life.
Grimaudan said that Danègre could not sell the pearl, so he must give it up within the hour. Or else he would post a letter to the prosecutor, in which the heiress named Danègre as the killer.

Night had fallen, and the two men walked in silence to the Parc Monceau, near the house of the countess. Danègre sank on a bench and said that the pearl lay between two paving stones, but first he wanted money for America.

Danègre told him to count the paving stones from the drain, and the pearl was between the twelfth and thirteenth. Grimaudan dug with his pocketknife, and about ten centimetres down he drew out the black pearl.

On the following day the Echo de France announced that Arsène Lupin had recovered the black pearl from the countess's killer. It added that copies of the jewel would soon be shown in London, New York and other cities.
Lupin told the writer that those forty minutes in the apartment were the most exciting of his life. He left a button so that a servant would be arrested, and took the knife and key as proof.

Lupin said that Danègre was still alive, and that he might have fallen into worse crimes if he had kept the pearl. Then he took the pearl from his wallet and wondered which rich prince or millionaire would own it one day.

In Sherlock Holmes Arrives Too Late, the banker Devanne tells his guest Velmont, a painter, that he looks like Arsène Lupin. Velmont is annoyed, and the guests laugh when Devanne says that only his cousin's recommendation stopped him from calling the police.

An officer said that the police had a full description of Lupin since his daring exploit on the Paris-Havre express. Devanne joked that Velmont's visits were a pleasant start to a more serious visit one night.
The Hall of the Guards held old chests, chandeliers and tapestries, and a huge bookcase with the name Thibermesnil in gold. Devanne told Velmont that tonight was his last chance to rob the castle.

Devanne announced, to his guests' great excitement, that Sherlock Holmes would arrive at four o'clock the next afternoon. He said that Lupin and his band were near, and that this time there had been no warning letter.
A month earlier a sixteenth-century book, the Chronique de Thibermesnil, had disappeared from Devanne's shelf. It held a plan of a secret passage from outside the walls into that very hall.

The police found no clue, so Devanne asked Sherlock Holmes for help, and the detective gladly accepted the challenge. The plan showed that the passage ended in the Tour Guillaume, but nobody knew the exact spot, for the secret was lost.

Father Gélis, the parish priest, said that two kings of France had known the secret. Henry the Fourth learned it the night before Arques, and his minister Sully later wrote a strange sentence about a bee.

Louis the Sixteenth had stayed there one night in 1784, and a paper in his handwriting had said Thibermesnil 3-4-11. Velmont laughed and said that Devanne had given him the missing key, so he must rob the castle that night.

Devanne drove Velmont to Dieppe, met three guests off the midnight train, and by one o'clock the castle was dark. At three o'clock something clicked in the Hall of the Guards, and a thin ray of light shot from a column of the bookcase.
A section of the bookcase turned on a pivot, and Arsène Lupin came in with eight men. He chose what to take, and they pushed armchairs, tapestries and paintings into the tunnel.

Lupin sent his men away with the furniture and kept only a motor-cycle for himself. He closed the bookcase, wiped away the footprints and forced open a glass cabinet of watches and rings in the gallery.
He was hanging some pearl bags on his arm when he heard a slight sound. A door opened above, and he hid behind a curtain as a woman came slowly down the stairs with a candle.

They stood face to face: it was Miss Nelly, the girl from the ship who had dropped his camera into the sea. Seeing himself as she must see him, a thief with full arms and pockets, he blushed and emptied everything into an armchair.

Nelly fled to the salon, and Lupin followed and promised that everything, even the furniture, would be returned tomorrow at three o'clock. She thought she heard footsteps and begged him to go, but when she came back from the door he had vanished.
Devanne soon guessed that Velmont was Lupin, but the idea seemed too absurd to tell the gendarmes. All morning the police searched the castle and found no sign of a break-in.
At eleven the officers arrived, and Devanne introduced his guests, including Miss Nelly Underdown. Velmont came late, at noon, and Devanne greeted him by saying that he had robbed the castle.

Coffee was served on the terrace while a regimental band played, and Nelly thought only of Lupin's promise. Her eyes kept returning to the great clock, and to Velmont, who was swinging calmly in a rocking chair.

The clock struck three, and two army wagons drove into the courtyard with all of Devanne's furniture, paintings and ornaments. The sergeant showed an order signed by a colonel, which an officer called a clever forgery.
Velmont asked Nelly whether he had not kept his promise, but she only looked at the ruby ring on his finger. It belonged to Devanne, and Lupin blushed and said that nothing could be changed.
Nelly walked past him into the house, and he never saw her again. A moment later he found her white rose on a flower box, and he picked up the fallen petals one by one.

Lupin left through a pine grove, jumped the park wall and took a path across the fields toward the station. In a narrow lane between two banks he met a tall, clean-shaven stranger with a heavy cane and a satchel.

The stranger asked, with a slight English accent, the way to the castle. Lupin said that Sherlock Holmes had no warmer admirer than himself, and the stranger stared at him so keenly that he felt photographed.

A group of gendarmes came down the lane, and the two men had to step back against the bank. Lupin wondered whether Holmes had recognised him, but the Englishman only brushed the dust from his clothes and said, “Thank you, monsieur.”

At first the people at the castle were disappointed by the commonplace look of the famous Englishman. Holmes grumbled that if his visit had not been announced, the robbery would not have taken place that night.

Holmes was ready to go home, but Devanne begged him to stay and explain how Lupin had come and gone. Holmes compared the two books, asked if Velmont had heard the two sentences, and said that Velmont and Lupin were the same man.

Holmes sat with his eyes closed, then knelt on the carpet and found fresh candle spots at the foot of the gallery stairs. He said that they explained why the goods were returned, but he must first see the passage, with a ladder and a lantern.

Holmes told Devanne to turn the first I of the word on the bookcase, then to move the B like a bolt. When Devanne opened the last I like a little gate, the whole bookcase turned, and he fell from the ladder.

Holmes explained that 3-4-11 meant the third, fourth and eleventh letters, a memory aid from Louis the Sixteenth, a clever locksmith. With a lantern the two men went down the steps and along the damp passage under the pond.

At the far end Holmes worked the three letters again, and a block of granite swung aside: the tomb of Duke Rollo. They were in the ruined chapel, and the chauffeur said that Velmont had told him to wait there for them.

In the car they found a package marked Sherlock Holmes, from Arsène Lupin, and it held Holmes's own watch. Holmes said nothing all the way to Dieppe, but at the station he vowed that he and Lupin would meet again.
C1C2: It was a strange end to a voyage that had begun so happily, for the liner La Provence was swift and comfortable and her captain was the most affable of men. Strangers who had never met the evening before now shared the same tables and decks, defying the anger of the ocean together, and a warm, spontaneous friendship grew up among them. Yet the little floating island was no longer cut off from the world, since the wireless telegraph, that invisible miracle of the air, whispered a few words from the receding coast to one passenger after another.

On the second day, five hundred miles from the French coast and in the midst of a violent storm, the wireless telegraph brought the ship a startling message. It warned that Arsène Lupin was in the first class, travelling alone, with fair hair, a wound on his right forearm and a false name that began with the letter R. At that moment a terrible flash of lightning tore the sky and broke the electric waves, so that the rest of the dispatch never arrived.

Although the officers would gladly have kept such news secret, it passed from mouth to mouth that very day, and soon every passenger knew that the famous Arsène Lupin was hiding among them. This was the elegant thief whom the newspapers adored and the police hated, the man who had once entered the house of Baron Schormann, left empty-handed and pinned up a card promising to return when the furniture was genuine. He had been a chauffeur, a bookmaker, a Russian doctor, a Spanish bullfighter and a feeble old man in turn, and he might now be anyone at all: the neighbour at dinner, or even the sharer of one's own cabin.

The next morning Miss Nelly Underdown declared that five more days with such a man in their midst would be unbearable, and she hoped that he would soon be arrested. She was one of those magnificent creatures who draw every eye, with wealth and beauty alike, and she was travelling with her friend Lady Jerland to visit her father, the millionaire Underdown of Chicago. Turning to Bernard d'Andrézy, who was known to be on friendly terms with the captain, she asked whether he had learned anything, and he wished that he had some news to please her.

He had meant at first to flirt with her, but in the growing closeness of the voyage his feelings had become too deep and respectful for that, and she seemed to accept his attentions with a certain favour. Yet he felt that he had a rival in a young man of quiet and refined tastes, whose silent humour she sometimes appeared to prefer to his own Parisian lightness. That morning, as they sat in their deck chairs under a sky washed clean by the storm, he suggested that the passengers could solve the mystery quite as well as the detective Ganimard, Lupin's sworn enemy.

Bernard pointed out that they held the key to the problem, since the thief had fair hair, travelled alone and gave a name beginning with R, so that the passenger list would reveal him by elimination. He drew the list from his pocket and found that, among all the men in the first class, just thirteen had names that began with that letter. Nine of those thirteen were accompanied by wives, children or servants, and so only four remained who were travelling alone.

The first was the Marquis de Raverdan, secretary to the American Ambassador, whom Nelly knew well, and the second was Major Rawson, whose nephew spoke up from the crowd. The third was Rivolta, an Italian whose face was hidden behind a heavy black beard, and Nelly burst out laughing, for nobody could call such a man fair. That left only the last name on the list, Monsieur Rozaine, and when Nelly turned to the quiet young man and asked why he did not answer, every eye turned to him.

Rozaine replied that, considering his name, his solitary journey and the colour of his hair, he had already reached the same conclusion and thought that he ought to be arrested. His thin lips were drawn tight, his face was ghastly pale and his eyes were streaked with blood, and although he was plainly joking, his manner struck everyone strangely. Nelly asked simply whether he lacked the wound, and he pulled back his sleeve to show his arm, but Bernard noticed that it was the left arm that he showed, and the message had spoken of the right.

Bernard was on the point of drawing attention to this when Lady Jerland, Nelly's friend, came running towards the group in a state of terrible excitement, crying that her jewels and pearls had been stolen. They had not all gone, as everyone soon discovered, for the thief had taken not the largest stones but the finest and most valuable ones, and the empty mountings lay upon the table like flowers whose petals had been plucked. It was a curious crime, and all the more alarming because it had been committed in the middle of the day.

The thief had struck in broad daylight, while Lady Jerland was taking tea, in a cabin that opened on a busy corridor, forcing the door and finding the jewel case at the bottom of a hat-box. Naturally every passenger reached the same conclusion, that it was the work of Arsène Lupin, and that evening the empty places on either side of Rozaine at the dinner table showed how far he was shunned. Later the rumour went round that the captain had placed him under arrest, and the news brought the passengers a feeling of safety and relief.

That evening the passengers resumed their games and dances, and Nelly in particular showed a spirit of thoughtless gaiety that proved she had forgotten any interest in Rozaine. At midnight, under a bright moon, Bernard declared his devotion with an ardour that did not seem to displease her. But next morning, to the general amazement, Rozaine was free, for he had produced documents showing that he was the son of a wealthy merchant of Bordeaux, and his arms bore not the slightest trace of a wound.

His enemies replied that Arsène Lupin could furnish as many certificates as anyone liked, that he had never had the wound or had removed it, and that a man of his talent could commit a theft without even being present. In any case, one question remained that no sceptic could answer: who else on board was travelling alone, was fair and bore a name beginning with R? When Rozaine came boldly towards the group a few minutes before breakfast, Nelly and Lady Jerland rose and walked away.

An hour later a handwritten notice passed from hand to hand among the sailors, stewards and passengers, announcing that Monsieur Louis Rozaine offered ten thousand francs for the discovery of Arsène Lupin or the stolen jewels. He added that if nobody would help him, he would unmask the scoundrel himself, and for the next two days he was seen wandering day and night, searching and questioning. The captain was just as active, and had the vessel searched from stem to stern, on the theory that the jewels might be hidden anywhere except in the thief's own cabin.

Nelly remarked that the thief, wizard or not, could not make diamonds invisible, and Bernard answered that all of Lady Jerland's jewels could be hidden in an apparatus no larger than the Kodak he used to photograph her. Meanwhile the captain's own watch had been stolen, and he was furious, and he watched Rozaine more closely than ever, until the next day the watch was found in the second officer's collar box. The joke astonished everybody and showed the humorous side of the thief, who seemed to combine business with pleasure like an author who nearly dies laughing at his own play.

On the following evening an officer on duty heard groans from the darkest corner of the ship, and there he found Rozaine lying with his head wrapped in a thick gray scarf and his hands tied with cord. A card pinned to his coat read that Arsène Lupin accepted with pleasure the ten thousand francs offered by Monsieur Rozaine, and the stolen pocket-book had in fact contained twenty thousand. Some said that Rozaine had attacked himself, but he could not have tied his own hands so, and the writing on the card matched Lupin's handwriting as printed in an old newspaper found on board.

Such was the terror among the passengers that no one would stay alone in a cabin or wander into an empty corner, and even close friends watched one another with distrust, for Lupin might now be anybody. Our last day on the steamer seemed endless, for everyone feared that this time it would be no mere theft but a murder, since the authorities were powerless and our lives were at the mercy of one man. Yet those hours were delightful for Bernard, because the frightened Nelly sought protection at his side, and inwardly he blessed Lupin for bringing them so close together.

As the ship approached the American shore, the search for the thief was quietly abandoned, and every passenger waited anxiously for the moment when the riddle would be solved. At last the gangway was placed in position, and Nelly, who was leaning on Bernard's arm and was almost fainting, watched the uniformed customs officers come on board. Bernard pointed out a little old man in an olive-green coat who stood at the foot of the gangway leaning on an umbrella, and he said that it was Ganimard, the celebrated detective who had sworn to catch Arsène Lupin.

The passengers began to leave the steamer, and Ganimard, leaning on his umbrella with an air of careless indifference, seemed to pay no attention to the crowd that hurried past him. Rozaine appeared at last, an American officer leaned forward and whispered something in the detective's ear, and Ganimard merely shrugged his shoulders and let him go. Bernard gave his camera to Nelly, since he was loaded down with luggage, but they had not gone ten steps when Ganimard barred their way and, gazing into his eyes, said calmly: Arsène Lupin, is it not?

Bernard laughed and said that he was simply Bernard d'Andrézy, but the detective replied that the real Bernard d'Andrézy had died in Macedonia three years before, and he gave a sharp blow to the young man's right arm. It struck the wound, still unhealed, that the telegram had described, and Bernard cried out and understood that he must surrender. He turned to Nelly, who had heard everything, and as their eyes met she glanced at the camera that hid the stolen jewels, then walked down the gangway and, pretending to be clumsy, let it fall into the water.

For a moment he stood motionless, wondering what she would do, and then, to Ganimard's great astonishment, he murmured that it was a pity he was not an honest man. Such was the story of his arrest as Lupin himself told it to the writer, who had since come to enjoy his friendship and the visits of a man for whom fate held only favours and smiles. Twenty times the writer had met Lupin and found a different man, and Lupin himself said that he could not recognise himself in the mirror, so long as the public could say: Arsène Lupin did that!

Every traveller on the Seine has noticed the little feudal castle of Malaquis, built upon a rock in the middle of the river and joined to the bank by an arched bridge. Its history is as stormy as its name and as harsh as its outlines, for the castle has known a long series of combats, sieges, assaults and massacres. Many mysterious legends cling to the place, and the best known tells of a tunnel that once led underground to the abbey of Jumièges and to the manor of Agnès Sorel, the mistress of Charles the Seventh.

In that ancient home of heroes and brigands lived Baron Nathan Cahorn, whom the Bourse had nicknamed Baron Satan, because he had made a fortune there with incredible speed. He lived alone, attended by three old servants, among a wonderful collection of furniture, wood carvings and porcelain, and no visitor ever saw his three Rubens, his two Watteau paintings or his pulpit by Jean Goujon. He loved them like a miser and guarded them like a jealous lover, and every evening at sunset the iron gates of the bridge were barred, so that the slightest touch set electric bells ringing through the castle.

One Thursday in September a postman with twinkling eyes handed the baron a registered letter, and the baron, who lived like a hermit and never had any mail, felt at once that it was an evil omen. He waited until the man had vanished round the bend of the road, walked nervously to and fro, and then leaned on the parapet of the bridge to open it. The sheet bore the heading Prison de la Santé, Paris, and at the bottom of the page, with a flourish, stood the name of Arsène Lupin.

Lupin wrote politely that a painting by Philippe de Champaigne pleased him beyond measure, that he liked the Rubens, and that he had noticed tapestries from Beauvais, a gueridon signed by Jacob and a cabinet of jewels. He asked the baron to pack them and ship them to Batignolles within eight days, otherwise he would remove them himself on the night of the twenty-seventh of September, and he would not stop at those things alone. A postscript added that the baron should not send the largest Watteau, since it was only a copy of a painting burned long ago, and that Lupin did not care for the chatelaine, because he doubted its authenticity.

The baron knew that Lupin was shut up in the Prison de la Santé, but he knew too that any miracle might be expected of such a man, and his exact knowledge of the castle alarmed him. He looked up at the stern walls, the steep rock and the deep water, and shrugged his shoulders, and yet he wondered what gate or drawbridge could stop Arsène Lupin once he had decided to come in. That evening he wrote to the prosecutor at Rouen, who replied that Lupin was closely watched and the letter was the work of an impostor, although an expert admitted certain resemblances to the prisoner's handwriting.

Two days passed, and then the baron read with joy in the Réveil de Caudebec that the veteran detective Ganimard, famous for capturing Arsène Lupin, was resting in the town and threatening to catch all the fish. Who could defeat the schemes of Lupin better than the patient and shrewd Ganimard? The baron did not hesitate, and after finding the office of the newspaper on the quay, he was told by the editor that the detective, a gruff little man in a straw hat, could be seen fishing under the trees.

The baron explained his case, and the fisherman listened without moving, his attention fixed on his rod, until at last he turned with profound pity and said that thieves do not usually warn their victims. He would gladly serve the baron, he said, if he had the least doubt about it, but that young man was already under lock and key, and nobody had ever escaped from the Santé. If Lupin did escape, so much the better, for he would simply catch him again, and meanwhile the baron should go home and sleep soundly, because he was frightening the fish.

For two days the baron checked his bolts and watched his servants and almost believed that his fears were groundless, but on the twenty-sixth of September a boy brought him a telegram. It said that no goods had arrived at Batignolles station and that he should prepare everything for the following night, so he hastened to Caudebec and offered the fisherman any price he liked. At the offer of three thousand francs Ganimard gave way, warning that the baron was throwing his money out of the window, and promised to bring two of his men at nine o'clock the next evening.

At half past eight the baron dismissed his servants, and soon Ganimard arrived with two assistants, great fellows with necks like bulls, whom he placed in the central gallery after barricading every door and window of the threatened rooms. He locked them in, took the keys, and led the baron to the old watchman's room in the thick outer wall, where one peep-hole looked on the bridge and another on the court. There he stretched himself across three chairs and lit his pipe, and when the baron heard a horn at one o'clock, Ganimard said it was only an automobile and went back to sleep.

At dawn all was calm, and the baron, radiant with joy, mounted the stairs behind Ganimard, who said that he felt ashamed to have accepted the money. Ganimard unlocked the gallery, and there upon two chairs, with drooping heads and hanging arms, his assistants were sleeping soundly. Then the baron cried out in horror, because the paintings, the tapestries and the jewels from the cabinets were gone, and he ran from one empty place to another, counting his losses and stamping with rage.

The famous detective did not move, for the windows were closed, the locks were intact, and there was no break in the ceiling or hole in the floor, so that the theft seemed to follow a logical and inexorable plan. He shook his assistants in vain and decided that they had been drugged, probably by the water in the carafe from which both admitted drinking, though he could find no taste or smell in it. The baron swore that he would pay any price to get his gems back, and Ganimard murmured that he had an idea, but that same day a complaint was filed against Lupin, prisoner in the Santé.

The baron soon regretted his complaint when he saw his castle given over to gendarmes, magistrates, photographers and a crowd of curious idlers, while the Echo de France, which somehow obtained the letter, published it for all to read. The officers searched the house from top to bottom, sounding the rock and exploring the cellars by torchlight, certain that a tunnel must exist, but they found no trace of one. At last the police of Rouen asked for help from Paris, and Monsieur Dudouis, chief of the Sûreté, spent two days at the castle without success before he sent for Ganimard.

Ganimard listened in silence to the orders of his chief, then shook his head and said that it was useless to ransack the castle, since the solution lay with Arsène Lupin. When Dudouis objected that the man was in prison, Ganimard answered that nobody else in France had the calibre to invent such a scheme, and that he would believe in the prison only when Lupin wore fetters and a gag. Hunting for secret passages and pivoting stones was nonsense, he added, for Lupin was a modern cracksman, and he asked permission to spend an hour in the cell, since they had become friendly on the journey back from America.

It was just after noon when Ganimard entered the cell, and Lupin, who was lying on his bed, raised his head and cried that his fondest wish in his chosen retreat had been to receive such a visitor. He praised Ganimard as almost as clever as Sherlock Holmes, regretted that he could offer only a hard stool and not even a glass of beer, and complained of the spies who ransacked his pockets ten times a day. Then he asked, with perfect good humour, to what he owed the visit, and when Ganimard answered that it was the Cahorn affair, he recalled at once the castle of Malaquis, the two Rubens, the Watteau and a few trifles.

Lupin declared that he had managed the whole affair from A to Z, the warning letter and the telegram included, and he added that he must still have the receipts somewhere. He opened the drawer of the little white wooden table that, with the bed and the stool, made up all the furniture of his cell, and handed Ganimard two scraps of paper. The detective was amazed that so closely watched a prisoner read newspapers and kept postal receipts, but Lupin only laughed, for the guards ripped open his waistcoat and sounded the walls without ever imagining so simple a hiding place.

Lupin said that he never wasted time on mere display, and that the letter had been the motor of the whole machine, for a castle that cannot be forced must somehow invite the thief to come in. A baron who received such a warning would write to the prosecutor, who would laugh at him because the burglar was in prison, and in his fear he would ask the first person he found for help. And if he read in a country newspaper that a famous detective was holidaying nearby, Lupin went on, he would run to that man, so the only task was to arrange that the newspaper should say so.

Lupin had asked a friend to visit Caudebec and let the editor of the Réveil understand that he was the famous detective, so that the baron, once he swallowed the bait, would beg that friend for help against Lupin himself. The false detective refused at first, but after the telegram he accepted the baron's money, and while he kept the baron busy, two men of the band lowered the treasures by rope into a hired launch. The name that had drawn the baron like a magnet was that of Lupin's own enemy, the illustrious Ganimard, who would find, if he went to the castle and the baron talked, that he had to arrest himself.

While the guard laid out his lunch, Lupin said calmly that the Cahorn affair was nearly settled, since the baron had probably recovered his pictures already, in return for a certain sum, and would withdraw his complaint. When Ganimard asked how he knew, Lupin answered that he had just received the telegram he was expecting, and invited him to break the egg on the tray. Mechanically the detective cracked the shell with the blade of a knife, and found inside nothing but a small piece of blue paper, a telegram that read, Contract closed, hundred thousand balls delivered, all well.

The hundred thousand balls, Lupin explained, were francs, which was little but times were hard, and Ganimard, whose ill humour had vanished, admitted that a dozen such men would force the police to close up shop. Lupin modestly replied that a man needs some diversion in his leisure hours, especially in prison, and then he repeated firmly that he had decided not to be present at his own trial. He added that nobody, not even Ganimard, could have laid a hand on him if a much more important event had not occupied his attention at that moment: a woman was looking at him, and he loved her.

He confessed that he had come to prison to rest his nerves, and he announced that on the following Wednesday, at four o'clock, he would smoke his cigar at Ganimard's house in the rue Pergolèse. Ganimard answered that he would expect him, and the two men shook hands like old friends who valued each other at their true worth. But as the detective reached the door, Lupin called him back and returned the watch that had strayed into his pocket, then showed him a large gold watch that had belonged to the examining judge, Jules Bouvier.

After his lunch, Lupin had taken from his pocket an excellent cigar with a gold band, and he was examining it with unusual care when the door of his cell opened. He had barely time to throw the cigar into the drawer of the table and step away from it before the guard came in to say that it was the hour for exercise. Lupin greeted the man as if he had been waiting for him all morning, and the two went out together along the corridor.

The moment the two men had turned the corner of the corridor, Inspectors Dieuzy and Folenfant entered the cell and began a minute examination, for they suspected that the prisoner was in touch with accomplices outside the walls. On the previous evening the Grand Journal had published a letter in his unmistakable handwriting, warning its court reporter that he would be called to account before the trial, and so Lupin plainly sent and received letters. The situation had become intolerable, and the chief of the Sûreté, Monsieur Dudouis, acting with the examining judge, had visited the prison and given the gaoler strict instructions.

They lifted every stone and searched the bed, as usual, and were about to give up when the guard hurried in to say that the prisoner had been closing the table drawer as he entered. Monsieur Dudouis was fetched and listed a bundle of newspaper cuttings about Lupin, a tobacco box, a pipe and two books, Carlyle's Hero-Worship in English and a charming old German translation of the Manual of Epictetus. Every page of both books was underlined and annotated, and he wondered whether they served as a code for correspondence or simply showed the studious character of their reader.

Dudouis took up the famous cigar and, like an habitual smoker, held it to his ear and squeezed it, and at once he cried out in surprise, for it gave way and something white showed between the leaves. With the aid of a pin he drew out a roll of very thin paper, scarcely larger than a toothpick, and unrolled it to find a message in a woman's handwriting. It said that the basket had taken the place of the others, that on pressing the outer foot the plate goes downward, and that H-P would wait every day from twelve to sixteen, and begged for a reply.

Dudouis reflected and said that it was clear: the basket had eight of its ten compartments ready, twelve to sixteen meant noon to four o'clock, and H-P, which describes the strength of a motor, meant an automobile. Since the cigar had not yet been touched, the prisoner must have received it that very day, perhaps hidden in his food, though the guard said that nothing had ever been found in what he ate. The chief took the letter to the examining judge, and they agreed to photograph it and to replace it within an hour in a cigar just like the first, so that the prisoner would suspect nothing.

In the evening Dudouis returned to the prison and examined three empty plates, telling Dieuzy to cut the macaroni into tiny pieces and open the bread roll, but found nothing there. He then examined the fork, the spoon and the knife, and when he turned the handle to the left and to the right it unscrewed, for the knife was hollow and held a folded paper. It was Lupin's reply, saying that he trusted his friend, that H-P should follow at a distance each day and that he would go ahead, and Dudouis rubbed his hands, sure of catching the whole band.

For several months the examining judge, Monsieur Bouvier, had struggled in vain, and the inquiry had shrunk to dull arguments with the famous advocate Maître Danval, while Lupin spoke only now and then, out of courtesy. One day he told the judge that the robbery of the Crédit Lyonnais, the false banknotes and the burglaries at Malaquis and other castles were all his own work, and ten times more besides. Once the two intercepted messages had been shown to the judge the examinations began again, and every day at noon Lupin was taken to the Dépôt in the prison van with other prisoners, returning at three or four o'clock.

One afternoon, since the other prisoners had not been examined, Lupin was taken back alone in a prison van, one of those vehicles that Parisians call salad baskets, with five small compartments on each side of a central corridor. A guard stood at one end, and Lupin, in the third compartment on the right, calculated every turn as the heavy van left the quai de l'Horloge and passed the Palais de Justice. About the middle of the Pont Saint-Michel he pressed with his right foot upon the metal plate that closed his cell, and something clicked and the plate moved, so that he saw he was sitting between the two wheels.

At the corner of the boulevard Saint-Germain the van stopped, because a truck horse had fallen and cabs and omnibuses had piled up, and Lupin slid the plate aside, set his foot on a spoke and leaped to the ground. A coachman saw him and roared with laughter, but his shout was lost in the noise of the traffic as it began to move again, and Lupin, with the air of an idle stroller, walked calmly up the boulevard. On the terrace of a café he ordered a beer, then sent for the owner and said loudly that he had forgotten his wallet, and he was Arsène Lupin, prisoner of the Santé and now a fugitive.

Lupin strolled through the rue Soufflot and the rue Saint-Jacques, looking into shop windows, until the high forbidding walls of the prison rose before him, and then he asked the sentinel if this was the Santé. When the man growled at him to move along, Lupin calmly said that he was Arsène Lupin and wished to regain his cell, and the sentinel, astonished, rang a bell and let him through the iron gate. Inside, the keeper pretended to be furious, but Lupin smiled and said that he knew the game, for twenty agents were following the van, and that when he wished to escape he would need no help.

Two days later the Echo de France, the official reporter of Lupin's exploits, published a complete account of the attempt, with the words of the messages, the walk along the boulevard and the scene at the café. It even revealed that the van had been prepared by his accomplices and substituted for one of the six vans used by the prison. When the judge joked about the affair, Lupin gave his word of honour that it was only the preliminary to his general plan, and added that further questions were useless, since he would not be present at the trial.

Lupin was moved to another cell, and the judge closed his inquiry, and for two months the prisoner lay almost constantly on his bed with his face to the wall, refusing to see his advocate. During the fortnight before the trial he took up a vigorous life again, and the public waited for his escape, while the Prefect of Police asked his secretary every morning whether he had escaped yet. On the day before the trial a gentleman walked into the office of the Grand Journal, threw his card in the court reporter's face and left, and the card said that Arsène Lupin always keeps his promises.

An enormous crowd of advocates, magistrates, reporters, actresses and fashionable women filled the court on a dark and rainy day, delighted at the thought of the pranks that the prisoner would play on the judge. In the dim light they saw a man who walked with a heavy, shambling step, dropped into his seat and looked passive and stupid, and who only shook his head when his advocate spoke to him. When the judge demanded his name, age and occupation and repeated the question, a thick, slow voice muttered, “Baudru, Désiré.”

The judge replied that, since the prisoner had used a dozen names already, he would keep the one the world knew, Arsène Lupin, whose early life was a mystery that might have included a conjuror's assistant. Perhaps, he added, the same man had been the cyclist who won a great prize and was never heard of again, a methodical apprentice preparing for his war against society. Under the strongest light the prisoner looked extremely thin, with hollow cheeks, an earth-coloured face and a straggling beard, and when the question was repeated twice he made a desperate effort and murmured the same name.

Ganimard gave his evidence in a nervous way, looking several times at the prisoner with obvious doubt, and twice he stopped, embarrassed, as if he feared to speak aloud the thought that troubled him. When the judge kindly offered to let him retire if he was ill, he asked permission to look at the prisoner at closer range, because there was some mystery about the man that he must solve. After several minutes of close examination he returned to the stand and declared solemnly, on his oath, that the prisoner before them was not Arsène Lupin, whose eyes had never been so alcoholic.

The judge, thunderstruck, adjourned the trial and sent for Monsieur Bouvier, the gaoler and the guards, and when the court sat again the first two declared that the accused bore only a very slight likeness to Arsène Lupin. One guard said that he thought it was he, but he had seen very little of the prisoner, who for two months had lain on his bed with his face to the wall in cell twenty-four. The poor man explained that he had been freed from the Dépôt, but two guards had seized him at the door and put him in the van, and he had not complained, since he ate and slept well.

The records showed that eight weeks earlier a man named Baudru Désiré had slept at the Dépôt and left at two o'clock, the very hour when Lupin, examined for the last time, left in the prison van. Baudru, a poor man who lived on alms in a rag-picker's hut, could not be kept in prison for ever, and Ganimard, sure that Lupin had played upon him like an instrument, had him freed and followed. On a foggy morning in January Baudru walked out of the gate, crossed the Seine and entered an omnibus waiting-room with a second exit, so that Ganimard, watching one door, lost both assistants and followed alone.

Alone now, Ganimard followed Baudru by omnibus and tram to La Muette and into the Bois de Boulogne, where the man wandered for an hour before sitting on a bench near a pond. After half an hour Ganimard lost patience, sat down beside him, lit a cigarette and remarked that it was a pleasant day, but there was no reply, and then the man burst into a happy, irresistible laugh. Ganimard felt his hair stand on end, for he knew that infernal laugh, and when he seized the man by the collar he saw behind the dull face the keen, mocking, youthful eyes of Lupin.

In a sudden fit of rage Ganimard seized Lupin by the throat, but with one slight movement Lupin made the detective's right arm fall useless, and remarked that the Japanese call that blow udi-shi-ghi. Ganimard said nothing, for he felt that his own evidence had led the court into serious error, and a tear rolled down to his gray moustache, but Lupin told him gently not to take it to heart. Appearance, Lupin explained, can be changed at will, and a few chemicals, two months of dieting, a thousand exercises and drops of atropine in the eyes had slowly turned him into Baudru, with no one noticing the change.

Baudru, Lupin said, was a real, harmless man whom he had copied, and his friends had made him sleep at the Dépôt, so that the police would find him and prefer to believe in a substitution. The van, the hollow cigar, the knife and the letters were only a bluff, he added, designed to make the public so sure of his escape that no one would ask whether the prisoner might be Lupin. Nobody would ever learn that Lupin had been the man discharged, he promised, and then he hurried off to dress, because he was dining that evening with the British Ambassador.

The evening before, the traveller had sent his automobile to Rouen by the highway, for he meant to go by rail to visit some friends who lived on the banks of the Seine. At Paris, a few minutes before the train started, seven gentlemen entered his compartment, most of them smoking, and since the carriage had no corridor, he gathered up his coat and papers and sought refuge next door. It seemed a small decision, yet it was to bring him a frightened lady, a mysterious stranger and one of the strangest adventures of his life.

The next compartment was occupied by a lady who, at the sight of the traveller, made a gesture of annoyance and leaned towards a gentleman standing on the step, evidently her husband. The gentleman looked the newcomer over and, finding his appearance reassuring, smiled and spoke to her like a man calming a frightened child, so that she smiled back and seemed to feel that she had nothing to fear. Her husband then said that he had an important appointment and could wait no longer, kissed her affectionately and left, and the whistle sounded and the train began to move.

At that moment, despite the protests of the guards, the door was flung open and a man rushed in, so that the lady, who was arranging her luggage, uttered a cry of terror and fell upon the seat. The traveller, who was not a coward, admitted that such intrusions at the last minute are always disconcerting, for they have a suspicious and unnatural air. Yet the newcomer was correctly and elegantly dressed, with a tasteful cravat and a refined, intelligent face, and the traveller felt certain that he had seen it before, though the memory was too vague to be recalled.

The traveller was amazed at the lady's pallor and anxiety, for she stared at their neighbour in alarm while one trembling hand crept towards a small travelling bag on the seat. Their eyes met, and he asked kindly whether she was ill, but she only gestured to show that she feared their companion, who looked at them both and then settled down in his corner. After a silence, as if summoning all her courage, she asked in an almost inaudible voice whether he knew who was on the train, and then breathed the name: Arsène Lupin.

He told her that Arsène Lupin had been sentenced the day before to twenty years of hard labour, and that the newspapers placed him in Turkey, so that he would hardly be so imprudent as to appear in public. The lady replied, plainly wishing the stranger to hear, that he was on this very train, for her husband directed the prison service and the stationmaster had told them that the police were searching for him. He had been seen in the waiting-room, she said, and had bought a first-class ticket for Rouen.

The lady explained that Lupin had vanished from the waiting-room without the guard at the door seeing him, and was supposed to have taken the express that left ten minutes after theirs. Unless, she added, he had leaped from that train into theirs, which seemed to her almost certain, although the traveller replied that he would then be arrested at Rouen. Never, she cried, for he would find some means of escape, and the traveller, smiling, said that in that case he wished him a good journey.

He unfolded his newspapers and read the reports of Lupin's trial, but they told him nothing new, and as he began to doze the lady seized his paper and asked indignantly whether he meant to sleep. He promised that he would not, and struggled to keep awake, but the landscape and the fleeting clouds grew confused, the nervous lady faded from his memory, and he sank into a profound sleep. In his dreams a creature bearing the name of Arsène Lupin leaped over walls and plundered castles, growing larger and larger, until he sprang into the compartment and landed squarely on the dreamer's chest.

With a cry of fright and pain he woke to find the stranger kneeling on his breast and gripping his throat, so that his eyes filled with blood, while the lady cowered, convulsed with terror, in the corner. He did not resist, for he lacked the strength, and the man loosened his grip, took a cord with a slip-knot ready and tied his wrists, so that in an instant the traveller was bound, gagged and helpless. And there he lay, wrapped up like a mummy, he, Arsène Lupin, seized and bound like a novice and soon to be robbed like a rustic, yet despite the danger he keenly appreciated the humour of it.

The thief did it all with the ease of a master, taking the traveller's purse and wallet and then the lady's bag, from which he removed the jewels and the gold trinkets. The lady opened her eyes, trembling, and drew the rings from her fingers and handed them to the man as if to spare him unnecessary trouble, and when he looked at her she fainted. Then, quite unruffled, he resumed his seat, lit a cigarette and examined his treasure with perfect satisfaction, while the traveller thought of the twelve thousand francs and the papers in his wallet.

He thought less of the twelve thousand francs, which he was certain he would recover together with his plans, addresses and compromising letters, than of the problem of how the affair would end. His friends at Rouen knew him as Guillaume Berlat and joked about his likeness to Arsène Lupin, so he had worn no disguise, and since his presence at Saint-Lazare had been remarked, the commissary at Rouen would certainly be waiting. No usual trick was possible now, for the commissary would find Arsène Lupin bound hand and foot, as docile as a lamb, ready to be delivered like a basket of fruit, while the train rushed toward Rouen.

Near Saint-Étienne the man rose, lowered the window and, since a heavy rain was falling, took the lady's umbrella from the rack and put on the traveller's overcoat. They were crossing the Seine when he turned up his trousers and lifted the outer latch of the door, and the helpless traveller wondered whether he meant to throw himself on the track. Then the train entered a tunnel and slowed for repairs, as the man seemed to know, and he stepped down, closed the door behind him and leaped to the ground.

The lady recovered her wits and lamented her jewels, but at the traveller's imploring look she quickly removed his gag, though he would not let her untie him, for the police must see everything as it stood. He told her to stand at the door at Rouen and call out, describing the thief in a soft hat, with her own umbrella and a gray overcoat, a coat that, he insisted, had certainly been the thief's. Above all, he added in a rather imperious tone, she must give his name, Guillaume Berlat, a friend of her husband, so that the inquiry would be hurried and the pursuit of Arsène Lupin begin at once.

As soon as the train stopped, several men entered the compartment, and Madame Renaud, panting, cried that Arsène Lupin had attacked them and stolen her jewels, and that her husband was a director in the prison service. She embraced her brother, a director of the Crédit Rouennais, and told the commissary through her tears that her friend Monsieur Berlat had been seized by the throat and that the thief had leaped from the train in the tunnel. He had been told of a hard felt hat, but she insisted it was soft, and when he mentioned a gray overcoat with a black velvet collar, she cried triumphantly that it was exactly right.

The police released him, and, stooping with a handkerchief over his bloody lips, he told the commissary weakly that it had been Arsène Lupin and that, if they hurried, he could still be caught. The railway car was detached as a silent witness, and the party was led to the station-master's office, where the traveller, seized by sudden doubt, decided to reach his automobile and escape before a telegram arrived from Paris. When asked to repeat his story, he said that Lupin was getting ahead of them and offered his automobile, but the commissary smiled and said that two of his men had already gone off on bicycles.

The traveller declared that Lupin was prowling round the station at Darnétal and would catch the train to Amiens at ten fifty, because he had consulted the railway guide to find a train near the place where he disappeared. The commissary congratulated him on so marvellous a deduction, though a slight suspicion crossed his mind, since the photographs of Lupin were too poor to resemble the man before him. Madame Renaud cried that the commissary must listen to Monsieur Berlat, and her words gave the name an identity no suspicion could touch, so that two men, Massol and Delivet, were assigned to help him.

In his swift Moreau-Lepton he felt a deep pride, for the motor answered his wishes, and he, free and out of danger, with two honest policemen behind him, was Arsène Lupin going in search of Arsène Lupin. Without Massol and Delivet, he reflected, he might often have taken the wrong road, but the end was not yet, for he still had to catch the thief and recover his papers without letting the policemen see them. They reached Darnétal three minutes after the train had left, and learned, with some consolation, that a man in a gray overcoat had boarded it with a second-class ticket for Amiens.

Delivet said that the express would reach Montérolier-Buchy in nineteen minutes, and that if the car did not arrive first the thief could escape, so they flew along the road for twenty-three kilometres. At a turn of the road they saw a vortex of smoke, the Northern Express, and for a kilometre it was a struggle side by side, but the issue was certain, and the car won by twenty lengths. In three seconds they stood on the platform, but the thief was not on board, and then he was seen crossing the track, and Massol, a runner of exceptional speed, chased him over a hedge and into a thick grove.

Massol was waiting at the edge of the grove, and the traveller, saying that their victim must be out of breath, sent him to the left and Delivet to the right, promising a pistol shot if he needed them. In truth he wished to arrest the fugitive alone, to recover his papers, about which the authorities would certainly ask a number of disagreeable questions. When the two had gone to their posts, he entered the grove with great caution, followed footprints on the wet grass to a mound crowned by a deserted hovel, and through an opening saw the man with his back turned.

In two bounds he was upon the man and threw him down before he could fire his revolver, holding him there with a knee on his breast. He whispered that he was Arsène Lupin and would spare him the police if he gave back the pocketbook and the jewels, and the man murmured yes. When the traveller rose, the man drew a large knife, and a sharp blow on the neck stunned him, after which the traveller recovered his papers and read on an envelope the name Pierre Onfrey, a wanted criminal.

He placed in an envelope two banknotes and a card thanking his worthy colleagues Massol and Delivet, and beside it left Madame Renaud's handbag, from which, business being business, he had taken everything of value. As the man began to wake, he fired the thief's revolver in the air to call his two assistants and hurried away through the ravine, and twenty minutes later he was sitting in his automobile. By six o'clock he was in Paris, where the evening papers announced that Pierre Onfrey had been captured at last, and the next day the Echo de France told how Arsène Lupin had arrested the criminal.

Two or three times a year, on occasions of unusual importance, the Countess de Dreux-Soubise wore upon her white shoulders the legendary necklace called the Queen's Necklace. It was the very necklace that Böhmer and Bassenge had made for Madame Du Barry, that Cardinal de Rohan had meant to give to Queen Marie-Antoinette, and that the adventuress Jeanne de la Motte had pulled to pieces in 1785. To tell the truth, only the mounting was genuine, for the beautiful stones had been scattered to the four winds.

Rétaux de Villette had kept the mounting while the Count and Countess de la Motte scattered the stones, and later he sold it to Gaston de Dreux-Soubise, nephew and heir of the Cardinal. Gaston bought back the few diamonds that remained with an English jeweller named Jeffreys and added other stones of the same size but inferior quality, thus restoring the necklace to its original form. For nearly a century the house of Dreux-Soubise had prided itself on this historic jewel, and although their fortune had shrunk, they preferred to cut their household expenses rather than part with a relic of royalty.

More than anyone, the present count clung to the necklace as a man clings to the home of his ancestors, and for safety he had rented a box at the Crédit Lyonnais in which to keep it. He went there himself on the afternoon of the day on which his wife wished to wear it, and he himself carried it back the next morning, so that it spent only a single night in the old house. Even so, that single night was to cause a drama that would trouble the house of Dreux-Soubise for years.

On the evening of the reception given at the Palais de Castille in honour of King Christian, the Countess de Dreux-Soubise achieved a remarkable success. The thousand facets of the diamonds sparkled like flames about her shapely neck and shoulders, and it is safe to say that nobody but she could have borne the weight of such an ornament with so much ease and grace. The king himself spoke of her beauty, and the count, who felt a double triumph, was highly elated as they drove home to their old house in the faubourg Saint-Germain.

When they reached their chamber the countess took the necklace from her shoulders, not without regret, and handed it to her husband, who admired it as passionately as if he had never seen it before. Having put it in its case of red leather stamped with the Cardinal's arms, he passed into a little alcove cut off from their chamber, which could be entered only by a door at the foot of their bed. As on earlier occasions, he hid the case on a high shelf among hat-boxes and piles of linen, closed the door, and went to bed.

Next morning the count went to the stables to see a sick horse, and when he returned he entered the cabinet and asked quietly whether his wife had taken the necklace, though she had not even opened that door. Together they threw the boxes to the floor and overturned the piles of linen, and when the candle had lit the emptied room, they confessed in despair that the famous necklace had disappeared. Without wasting time on lamentations, the countess sent for the commissary of police, Monsieur Valorbe, who came at once and asked whether anyone could have passed through their chamber in the night.

The count answered that he was a very light sleeper and that the door of their chamber had been bolted, and he remembered unbolting it that morning when his wife rang for her maid. Monsieur Valorbe examined the only other opening, a window onto a small inner court, which had been covered by a narrow press, and when the press was moved, the window was found fastened, so no one had entered that way. Asked whether any servant knew that the necklace was kept in the cabinet, the countess said that nobody did, and then, after some hesitation, she added that she had been thinking of Henriette.

Henriette, a school friend of the countess who had been disowned for marrying beneath her, lived in a wretched apartment in the house, sewing for the countess while her son Raoul, about six years old, sat beside her reading. She was overwhelmed to hear of the theft, and she laughed at the idea of being suspected, pointing out that she never left her room and that the opposite window lay at least three metres from her kitchen. Yet when asked how she knew that the necklace had been in the cabinet, she said that it had been mentioned in her presence, and her face grew anxious as she drew her son towards her.

The commissary handed the case to the examining judge, who questioned the servants, tested the bolt, tried the window and explored the little court, but the bolt was intact and the window could not be opened from outside. Because the inquiries kept turning towards Henriette, her past life was searched, and it was found that in three years she had left the house only four times, always for reasons that were satisfactorily explained. After a week the judge said that even if they knew the culprit they could not tell how the theft was done, since a bolted door and a fastened window left no way in and no way out.

At the end of four months the secret opinion of the judge was that the count and countess, who as usual were hard pressed for money, had sold the Queen's Necklace themselves, and he closed the investigation. The loss was a severe blow, for their credit, no longer propped up by such a treasure, was attacked by more demanding creditors, and they had to sell or mortgage everything of value. They would have been ruined if two large legacies from distant relatives had not saved them, but their pride suffered as if they had lost a quartering from their coat of arms.

Strangely, it was on her former schoolmate that the countess vented her spite, accusing her openly, sending her first to the servants' quarters and dismissing her the next day. For some time the count and countess led an uneventful life, travelling a good deal, until, some months after Henriette's departure, the countess was astonished to receive a letter from her thanking her for something that she had sent. Questioned about it, Henriette explained that she had received by post two banknotes of a thousand francs, in an envelope with a Paris postmark and a disguised handwriting, and the countess knew nothing about them.

Henriette received a similar letter and a like sum twelve months later, and a third time and a fourth, each year for six years, with this difference, that in the fifth and sixth years the amount was doubled. When the post office seized one letter because it was not registered, the last two were sent in proper form, from Saint-Germain and from Suresnes, and the writer signed them with the names Anquety and Péchard, giving false addresses. At the end of six years Henriette died, and the mystery of the necklace and of the money remained unsolved.

Years afterwards the Count de Dreux-Soubise gave a dinner for several ladies and a group of gentlemen, among them the deputy Bochas, the old General Marquis de Rouzières and the Chevalier Floriani, whom he had met in Sicily. Over coffee the talk turned to famous crimes, which gave the Marquis, who loved to tease the count, a chance to mention the Queen's Necklace, a subject that the count detested. Each guest offered his own opinion, and the theories were as contradictory as they were impossible, until the countess turned with a smile to the quiet Chevalier Floriani.

Floriani modestly said that he had no opinion, but when the count had unwillingly told the whole story, he listened, reflected and remarked that at first sight the problem was very simple. There was only one positive fact, he explained, for a bolted door cannot be opened from outside, so the thief must have entered by the window. When the count objected that the window had been found fastened, Floriani went on calmly that the thief had only to build a bridge, a plank or a ladder, between the kitchen balcony and the ledge.

Floriani asked whether the window had a transom above it and explained that through a hole in the putty at the side a person with a poker bent into a hook could catch the ring and pull the transom open. The count laughed and said that there was no hole, for it would have been seen, but Floriani replied that nobody had looked, and the count, much excited, paced the room and then rushed out. When he returned, pale and trembling, he stammered that the hole was there, at the very spot, and seizing the Chevalier's arm he demanded that he go on and tell the rest.

He went on that, if no man could crawl through the transom, it must have been a child, and he reminded them that Henriette had a son named Raoul. For a bridge, he said, the boy would have used something close at hand, such as the shelves where his mother kept her pans, and perhaps the bent poker lay still beside the stove. The count left the room again, and this time the guests were calm and confident, so that nobody was surprised when he returned and declared that the shelves had been unnailed and the poker was there.

The countess exclaimed that the mother must have compelled her son, but the Chevalier answered that all this had happened in the next room, during the night, while the mother slept.
