The necklace, he added, would have been found in the child's desk among his school-books, had the commissary looked there instead of wasting his time on an innocent mother. As for the money Henriette received, it proved nothing against her, for she was watched, while the child, who was free, could sell one diamond or two to a dealer and have the money sent from Paris.

Floriani said that he only pictured the mother's illness, the boy's schemes to sell the stones to save her, and the man who returns to the house where his mother was accused. The count, pale, asked who he was, and the Chevalier answered that he was only the guest whom the count had met at Palermo, and that his story was a mere pastime. But as he half rose and bowed to the countess, there could be no doubt that he was Henriette's son, and that he wished to be recognised.

The count hesitated, for he could ring for his servants and make a scandal, but he decided to pretend that he did not understand, and asked with a mocking smile whether the young man had abandoned so brilliant a career. To steal the Queen's Necklace at six years of age, replied Floriani in the same spirit, had cost the boy no trouble at all, for he had only to reach out his hand, or rather both hands. When the countess remarked that the son of such a woman had followed his nature, he told her that most of the diamonds were false, and she answered haughtily that it was still the Queen's Necklace.

Trembling with humiliated pride, the countess told him to tell that man that, although the stones had been removed, the Queen's Necklace still belonged to the house of Dreux-Soubise as much as its name or its honour. The Chevalier replied simply that he would tell him, bowed to her, saluted the count and the other guests and departed. Four days later the countess found on her table a red leather case bearing the Cardinal's arms, and the next day the Echo de France announced that Arsène Lupin had recovered the necklace and returned it.

The writer of this story, then a reporter on the Gil Blas, owed his friendship with Arsène Lupin to chance alone, for chance placed him in one of the thief's strangest and most mysterious adventures. On the memorable night of 22 June he dined with friends at the Cascade restaurant, where, to the sound of melancholy waltzes, they talked only of crimes and dark intrigues, a poor overture to a night's sleep. The Saint-Martins drove away in an automobile, and the delightful, heedless Jean Daspry walked home with him through the warm dark night to his little house on the boulevard Maillot at Neuilly.

At the door Daspry asked whether he was afraid, for the house was so isolated, with nothing around it but vacant lots, and he admitted that the stories had unsettled him too. They shook hands and said good night, and the writer opened the door on a dark, silent hall, where he remembered with annoyance that his servant Antoine had been given a short leave of absence. He climbed the stairs on tiptoe, bolted his bedroom door, and, although the candle restored his courage, took care to place his large revolver beside the bed.

He lay down and took a book from the night-table to read himself to sleep, but instead of the paper-knife that marked his place he found an envelope closed with five seals of red wax. It was addressed to him and marked Urgent, and with nervous fingers he opened it and read that, whatever happened and whatever he might hear, he must not move or utter one cry, or he was doomed. He told himself that it was a joke, the work of some cheerful idiot, and he tried to laugh, but some haunting fear compressed his throat.

He did not even blow out the candle, but lay listening until he heard a slight noise, followed by crackling sounds, from the large room that he used as a library. He longed to seize his revolver, but then he saw one of the curtains move, and in the space behind it stood a bulky human form that kept the curtain from hanging straight. The man could see him through the meshes of the curtain, and he understood that this man was set to guard him while the others carried off their booty.

Then came a terrific noise that shook the house, followed by lighter sounds like a rebounding hammer, and the whole uproar proved that the intruders were not only bold but sure of being undisturbed. He did not move, not so much from cowardice as from a total weakness of the limbs, joined to the thought that ten others might stand behind the guard and that no life was worth risking for a few tapestries. Throughout the night his torture endured, with his eyes fixed on the guard and his heart beating wildly, until the sound of a milk wagon on the boulevard brought him immense relief.

At last daylight stole into the room, carriages passed along the boulevard, and the phantoms of the night vanished, so he put one arm out of bed, fixed his eyes on the curtain, seized his revolver and fired. He leaped from his bed with a cry of deliverance and ran to the window, where he found that the bullet had passed through the curtain and the glass but had touched no one, for there was nobody there. All night he had been hypnotised by a fold of the curtain, and, furious, he rushed through the antechamber into the library, convinced that the thieves had carried everything away.

He stopped on the threshold, astounded, for the furniture, books, paintings and tapestries that he supposed stolen were all in their places, with no clue to the intruders, not a chair disturbed, not the trace of a footstep. He made a tour of the walls and a mental inventory of every familiar object, and pressing his hands to his bewildered head, he told himself that he could not be mad, for he had certainly heard something. Inch by inch he searched the room, and at last, under a small Persian rug, he found a playing card, a seven of hearts, with this strange difference, that each of its seven hearts was pierced by a round hole.

All day he searched the library, a room much too large for the house, with a mosaic floor and walls of coloured panels, one of which showed an emperor with a golden crown, a long beard and a sword. Quite high up there was a large window that stayed open at night, but the soft earth beneath it bore no mark of a ladder, and there were no footprints anywhere in the yard. He did not tell the police, who would have laughed, but as a reporter he wrote a long account for the Gil Blas, which was taken for fiction, although Jean Daspry studied the affair and reached no conclusion.

A few mornings later Antoine announced a gentleman who would not give his name, a man of about forty with a dark complexion and lively features, whose correct but frayed clothes contrasted strangely with his rough manners. Without preamble he said that the article had interested him very much and that he might have information, but first he wished to be sure that every fact was exactly as related. The only way to be sure, he said, was to stay alone in the library for three minutes, because certain details matched another case he knew, and the writer, curious but not alarmed, agreed.

He went downstairs and took out his watch, and as the minutes passed, they seemed strangely solemn, until, after two minutes and three quarters, he heard a pistol shot. He bounded up the stairs and entered with a cry of horror, for the man lay motionless on his left side in the middle of the room, with a wound in his forehead and a smoking revolver beside him. Two feet from the body, upon the floor, lay a playing card, which he picked up, and it was a seven of hearts, each of its seven spots pierced with a small round hole.

Half an hour later the commissary of police arrived, then the coroner and the chief of the Sûreté, Monsieur Dudouis, and the writer took care not to touch the body. The first inquiry disclosed nothing, for there were no papers in the dead man's pockets, no name on his clothes and no initial on his linen, and the room was in the same perfect order as before. But as two policemen raised the body to place it on a stretcher, a crumpled card fell from the left hand, bearing the words: Georges Andermatt, thirty-seven rue de Berry.

Georges Andermatt was a rich banker, the founder and president of the Metal Exchange, who lived in princely style with numerous automobiles and an expensive racing stable, and whose wife was noted for her grace and beauty. Dudouis, seeing that the dead man was not the thin, greying banker himself, telephoned him from the vestibule, and twenty minutes later Monsieur Andermatt arrived in his automobile. After the circumstances were explained to him, he looked at the body with considerable emotion and said in a low voice that it was Etienne Varin, whom he knew only by sight, and who had a brother, Alfred.

Monsieur Andermatt said that he had told all he knew and could not explain how his card came to be in the dead man's hand, and although everyone expected it to reveal the truth, he gave no explanation. The investigation showed that the Varin brothers were Swiss, had lived under various names, frequented gambling halls and mixed with a band of foreigners broken up by the police, and nobody knew what had become of them. The writer thought the case too complicated ever to be solved and decided to waste no more time on it, but Jean Daspry grew more interested every day.

Daspry pointed out a foreign news item: the first trial of a new submarine, which might revolutionise naval warfare, would be held in secret before the former Emperor, and an indiscretion had revealed its name, the Seven-of-Hearts. The writer wondered whether any connection could exist between that name and the strange events in his house, but Daspry said that the most diverse effects often proceed from the same cause. Two days later a second report said that the plans had been prepared by French engineers who, after seeking support from their compatriots in vain, had approached the British Admiralty, also without success.

In the Echo de France an article signed Salvator told how, ten years before, a young mining engineer named Louis Lacombe had resigned his post and rented number 102 boulevard Maillot, the very house in which the writer lived. Through the Varin brothers of Lausanne, one of whom helped with his experiments while the other acted as agent, he met Georges Andermatt, who promised to win the support of the Minister of Marine. After two years, on the day when Lacombe asked the banker to approach the Minister, he dined at Andermatt's house and left about half past eleven at night, and he has never been seen since.

The article stated that the plans of Louis Lacombe were now in the hands of the Varin brothers, who had sold them to a foreign power, but that the foreign trials had failed, for the final document was missing. Andermatt, it went on, knew of this document, and must explain why he had hidden these facts when Etienne Varin died and why for six years he had paid spies to watch the brothers. He must answer in acts as well as words, and at once, it concluded, for otherwise, and there the threat ended, while the paper announced that willing or not, the banker would now be its collaborator.

That evening the writer and Daspry were dining among the newspapers, discussing the affair like men who keep falling over the same obstacles, when the door opened and a lady with a thick veil entered. She had come by the servants' entrance, though nobody knew how she knew the way, and when she raised her veil they saw a brunette with regular features, not handsome but attractive, above all for her sad dark eyes. She said that she was Madame Andermatt and had come hoping for information about the affair, but beneath her tranquil manner the writer sensed some poignant grief.

She answered every question, saying that she had known Lacombe through her husband, that she had last seen him on the evening he dined with them, and that he had spoken vaguely of a journey to Russia. When he left, he carried a satchel with all his papers, and two days later her husband learned that the Varin brothers held them, but he did not denounce them, because the satchel had held something more than papers. Blushing, she admitted that she had written other letters to Lacombe, that the Varin brothers held them, and that Alfred Varin threatened to publish them if her husband acted, so that he feared a scandal and they lived like strangers.

She told them that the hiding-place was in this very house, in one of the safes that Lacombe might have built, and that her husband had forced it on the night of 22 June and left his card. Daspry thought the theory simple but wrong, for the visitor of 22 June had been the mysterious man who held all the threads and wrote to the Echo de France as Salvator. He urged her to write to Salvator at once, confiding in him without reserve, since their interests were the same, and to try to get for him the document that completed the plans, which her husband held.

Two days later Madame Andermatt sent them the reply that she had received from Salvator, a short note saying that he had not found the letters, but would get them, and that she should rest easy. The writer looked at it and recognised the handwriting of the letter that he had found in his book on the night of 22 June, so Daspry was right, and Salvator was the author of the whole affair. Some points were becoming clearer, but others remained obscure, above all the two pierced cards and the fact that a submarine built from Lacombe's plans bore the name of the Seven-of-Hearts.

Daspry gave little thought to the two cards and turned instead to the problem he thought more urgent, the famous hiding-place, hoping to find the letters that Salvator might have missed. In a short time the large room held no more secrets for him, so he examined the other rooms, the foundation stones, the bricks of the walls and even the slates of the roof. One day he arrived with a pickaxe and a spade, gave the spade to the writer and led him to the vacant lots next door, where a small pile of earth and gravel covered with briers caught his attention.

For an hour they laboured under a hot sun without success, until at last Daspry's pickaxe unearthed some bones, the remains of a skeleton with scraps of clothing still clinging to it. Then the writer, turning pale, found in the earth a small rectangle of iron, the size of a playing card, with seven spots of red lead arranged like the seven of hearts, each pierced by a round hole. He told Daspry that he had had enough and went home to bed, where for forty-eight hours he lay feverish and haunted by dancing skeletons that threw their bleeding hearts at his head.

Daspry came every day and spent hours in the large room, tapping and ferreting, saying from time to time that the letters were there and that he would stake his life on it. On the third day the writer rose, weak but cured, and that afternoon a letter arrived from Salvator, who announced that the drama begun on 22 June was drawing to a close. He asked to bring the two chief actors face to face in the writer's house between nine and eleven that evening, and reminded him that on 22 June he had taken excellent care of his property.

He was amused by the facetious tone of the letter and would not betray such confidence, but he meant to watch, so he gave his servant a theatre ticket and left the garden gate unlocked. A few minutes later Daspry arrived and read the letter, and asked whether he meant to leave the house as Salvator asked, but the writer answered that he would be discreet and stay. Daspry, laughing, said that he was right and that he would stay too, for he would not miss it for anything.

The bell rang twenty minutes early, and the writer opened the door to Madame Andermatt, faint and nervous, who stammered that her husband was coming to an appointment where he would be given the letters. A servant had handed her a message for her husband at dinner, and before he snatched it away she read that he must come at nine with the papers, in exchange for the letters. The writer led them to the large room, where all three could hide behind the velvet curtain of the chimney, and at nine o'clock the garden gate creaked on its hinges.

Someone entered, and the writer recognised Alfred Varin at once, for he had the same slouching gait and the same cadaverous face and black beard as his brother Etienne. He entered with the nervous air of a man who fears traps, and the velvet curtain of the chimney seemed to displease him, but he climbed on a chair to feel the outline of the mosaic king. Suddenly he leaped down and moved away, for he had heard footsteps, and Monsieur Andermatt appeared at the door.

The banker cried out in surprise, asking whether Varin had summoned him, but Varin protested that a letter signed by Andermatt had brought him there, and the banker swore that he had written nothing. Varin, put on guard against the unknown enemy who had drawn him there, glanced toward the chimney again and walked to the door, saying that he did not like the affair and was going home. But Andermatt barred his way, saying that he had something to say to him and that this was a good time to say it, and Varin, recoiling before his resolute manner, muttered that he should be quick.

Andermatt told Varin that now, when he had nothing more to fear, he could say what he had done with Louis Lacombe, for on the last night he saw him he had noticed two men slinking away in the shadows. Varin said that the papers had simply been found on Lacombe's table, but the banker called that a lie, since two days later Varin had offered to sell him the plans. Then each accused the other of wanting the letters, Varin laughing that he could not part with them, and Andermatt declared that Varin would not leave the house until he handed them over.

Varin drew a revolver and, pointing it at the banker, demanded yes or no, and as Andermatt stooped, a pistol shot sounded close to the writer and the weapon fell from Varin's hand. It was Daspry who had fired, and in a moment he stood between the two men and told Varin with a sneer that he had been lucky, for he had aimed at his hand and struck only the revolver. Telling Varin that it was now between the two of them, that hearts were trumps and that he played the seven, he held up before the man's bewildered eyes the little iron plate with seven red spots.

Livid, with staring eyes, Varin seemed hypnotised by the sight of the plate, and he gasped, who are you, and Daspry answered that he was one who meddled in other people's business down to the bottom. In a voice of unexpected authority he said that Varin had been told to bring all the papers taken from Lacombe and sold to Major von Lieben, and Varin, conquered, touched his pocket and said that he had the originals. He asked a hundred thousand francs, but Daspry replied that the major had paid only twenty thousand and the boat had failed, and after a short haggle they agreed on ten thousand.

Daspry asked the banker to sign a check for the amount, and when Andermatt objected that he had no checkbook, Daspry handed him one, which the astonished banker recognised as his own. Told to waste no words, Andermatt filled in the check and signed it, and Varin held out his hand for it, but Daspry told him to put it down, because there was something more. Then he reminded the banker that he had asked for a packet of letters, and he demanded of Varin where the letters were, though Varin said that his brother had kept them.

Varin claimed that the letters were not in the hiding-place, but when Daspry handed him the iron plate and told him to open it, he recoiled in terror and cried that he would not. So Daspry climbed on a chair himself and fitted the plate to the king's sword so that its edges matched exactly, then pressed seven little mosaic stones with an awl through the seven holes. As he pressed the seventh a click was heard, and the whole bust turned on a pivot and showed a large steel-lined opening, a fire-proof safe, which was empty.

Varin said that his brother must have taken the letters, but when Daspry insisted that there was another hiding-place and the banker agreed to pay ten thousand francs, Varin closed the safe and took up the plate again. He thrust the awl into each hole, and there was the same click, but this time only part of the safe turned, and a very small safe appeared, built into the door of the large one. In it lay a packet of letters tied with tape and sealed, which Varin handed to Daspry, who asked the banker whether the check was ready and whether he had the last document from Lacombe.

The exchange was made, and Daspry pocketed the document and the checks and offered the packet of letters to Monsieur Andermatt, saying that this was what he had wanted. The banker hesitated, as if afraid to touch the cursed letters that he had sought so eagerly, and then took them nervously, while beside the writer there came a moan, and he found Madame Andermatt's hand cold. Daspry said that he wanted no thanks, since it was only by chance that he had been able to do the banker a good turn, and wished him good night, and the banker went out carrying his wife's letters.

Delighted that all was going well, Daspry examined the papers carefully and put them in his pocket, but when Varin eagerly asked for the checks, he answered that nobody could ask payment for returning papers that he had stolen. Varin, wild with rage, demanded the money, but Daspry gripped his arm until he cried out and suggested that they walk to the vacant lot nearby, where a little mound of earth hid more than he thought. The iron plate had come from there, Daspry said, for the brothers had buried it with the body and with other things that would interest a judge, and Varin covered his face and muttered that he was beaten.

Varin asked whether a little casket had been in the large safe on 22 June, and Daspry said that it had, full of diamonds and pearls collected by the brothers, and that of course he had taken it. Varin understood that it was the loss of the casket that had driven his brother to kill himself, and then, thinking of revenge, he asked the man's name. He staggered as if struck by a heavy blow at the answer, for those two words deprived him of all hope: Arsène Lupin.

Daspry pushed Varin through the door, and when the writer called that Madame Andermatt was ill, he hurried to her and made her breathe some salts, and learned that she had fainted when he handed her letters to her husband. He struck his forehead, cried that he was an imbecile, since of course she would think so, and drew from his pocket a small package exactly like the one that the banker had carried away. The letters in her husband's hands, he explained, were only copies, rewritten by himself in careful words, that the banker would never suspect, since they had been taken from the safe in his presence.

Madame Andermatt thanked him as she would a gentleman of her own circle, for she had not heard the last scene, but the writer was stunned to learn that his club companion was Arsène Lupin. Daspry said, quite at his ease, that the writer could say farewell to Jean Daspry, who was going to Morocco, where he might find a death worthy of him, as he expected. But Arsène Lupin, he added, would remain, for he was only at the threshold of his career, and he expected great things.

He had found the smaller safe only the afternoon before, while the writer slept, and it was simple enough, for the old emperor in mosaic was an exact portrait of the king of hearts on every playing card. Because he had always placed the plate the same way, it had opened only the larger safe, but by turning it upside down he changed the pattern of the seven spots on the mosaic and found the second hiding-place. On the night of 22 June he had known that the seven of hearts was the key to a casket, and he had turned the dinner talk to crimes so that his friend would be too nervous to leave his bed.

Daspry wrote one of those short articles that amused and mystified the public, announcing that Arsène Lupin had given all of Lacombe's plans to the Minister of Marine and headed a subscription for the first submarine built from them. His own subscription was twenty thousand francs, and when the writer cried that this was the banker's check, Lupin answered that it was quite right that Varin should redeem his treachery. That is how the writer came to know Arsène Lupin, and how, thanks to his confidence, he became his very humble and faithful historian.

At three o'clock in the morning, after a party on the boulevard Berthier, one of the last guests walked home through a clear, cold winter night, and soon he had the disagreeable feeling that someone was following him. When he turned he saw a man skulking among the trees, and as he reached for his revolver the man rushed at him, threw him down on a pile of gravel and gagged him with a handkerchief. Just as his eyes were closing, a stranger attacked the man with a cane and a boot, so that he fled limping and cursing, and the stranger bent over him and asked whether he was hurt.

By the time they reached the avenue de la Grande-Armée he was quite recovered, and he overwhelmed his rescuer with thanks, promising that his wife would thank him in person at breakfast the next day. He gave his name as Ludovic Imbert and asked for his rescuer's, and the stranger smiled and handed him a card bearing the name Arsène Lupin. At that time the name meant nothing to anyone, for it had been invented for this occasion, and it was in this affair that Arsène Lupin was baptised, an apprentice in a profession where he soon became a master.

He had prepared a special costume for the occasion, a shabby frock-coat, baggy trousers and a frayed silk hat, all correct in form but marked with the stamp of poverty, and a cravat pinned with a false diamond. On the tram he met the lodger from the third floor, who had played the attacker, and told him that it was all fixed, for he had not staged the assault to waste a rescue so well planned. For six months he had studied the affair, questioning servants and money-lenders and shadowing husband and wife, and he knew that the fortune, whatever its source, was real, and that the safe held bonds worth perhaps five million francs.

Madame Gervaise Imbert, a short, plump and very talkative woman, said that she had wanted to entertain their saviour alone, and from the first they treated him as an old and valued friend. Lupin told them of his life, his father the magistrate and his sad childhood, while Gervaise described the kindness of the aged Brawford and the hundred millions she had inherited, which lawsuits with his nephews kept her from enjoying. The bonds were there in her husband's safe, she said, and if they detached one coupon they would lose everything, and Lupin shivered at his nearness to so much wealth.

The unfortunate young man was soon made private secretary to the couple at a hundred francs a month, with a room on the second floor directly above Ludovic's office, and he quickly saw that the post was a sinecure. He was never invited to their parties, but he did not complain, and he paid secret visits to the office to inspect the safe, an immense block of iron and steel that no burglar's tools could force. Lupin was not discouraged, for where force fails, he told himself, cunning prevails, and he had only to watch and wait for his chance.

He drilled a lead pipe through the floor of his room into the ceiling of Ludovic's office, and from then on he spent his days stretched on the boards, watching the couple at their safe. He tried to learn the figures of the combination and wondered where they hid the key, and one day, seeing them leave the safe unlocked, he ran down and entered boldly, but they had already returned. Far from suspecting him, they asked his advice about which bonds to sell, and that afternoon Ludovic took him along and sold some annuities to a stockbroker for forty-six thousand francs.

Lupin felt out of place in the Imbert house, for the servants never knew his name and called him only monsieur, and the couple, after their first enthusiasm, treated him as an eccentric who liked solitude. Once he heard Madame Imbert call him a barbarian, and he decided that, very well, he was a barbarian, and when newspapers accused the Imberts of swindling he knew that he could not wait much longer. For five evenings he locked himself in his room and lay watching Ludovic's office, until on the sixth day he learned that the Imberts meant to make an inventory of the safe that night.

After dinner the Imberts began to examine their books and the securities in the safe, and as the servants went upstairs, they were still at work at midnight. Then Lupin tied a knotted rope to his balcony and descended in silence to the office window, which he had so arranged that afternoon that the bolt would not catch. Through the curtains he saw the couple murmuring in front of the safe, and he was about to rush in when Madame Imbert said that the room was cold and that she would go to bed.

Half an hour later Ludovic rose to close the window, and then, without a cry or a struggle, Lupin stunned him, wrapped the curtain about his head and bound him hand and foot. Quickly he opened the servants' gate to a waiting carriage, and with the coachman emptied the safe in two trips, then went back to his room and removed the rope and every trace of his work. Next morning the newspapers announced that Ludovic and Gervaise Imbert had disappeared, and when the officers of the law opened the safe, they found there what Lupin had left, which was nothing.

Later, in a confidential mood, Lupin told the writer the sequel, and when asked if he felt remorse for stealing their fortune, he cried that the bonds were counterfeit, every one, and not worth a sou. While he posed as their saviour, he said, they had passed him off as Brawford, the eccentric barbarian shown only at a distance, and on the strength of his name they had borrowed from the bankers. He added, in a grotesque rage, that Gervaise Imbert owed him fifteen hundred francs, his savings, wormed out of him for imaginary charity, and that it was the first time he had been played for a fool.

At three o'clock in the morning a violent ringing woke the concierge of number nine, avenue Hoche, and a voice asked for Doctor Harel on the third floor, although she warned that he never went out at night. The visitor climbed past the doctor's door to the fifth floor, where he tried two keys, one of which fitted the lock, and he murmured that this simplified the business wonderfully. Then, to prepare his retreat, he waited ten minutes, as if he had been dismissed by the doctor, and went noisily down the stairs, grumbling about physicians, so that the concierge heard him go.

As he left, he slipped a piece of iron into the street door so that the bolt could not catch, and unknown to the concierge he went quietly back in, with his retreat assured. On the fifth floor, by lantern light, he put his hat and overcoat on a chair, covered his heavy shoes with felt slippers and remarked that burglary was a delightful profession for those with care and reflection. Then he unfolded a detailed plan of the apartment and located himself: on the street front lay the drawing-room, boudoir and dining-room, where he would not waste time, since the countess had a deplorable taste and nothing of value.

He folded his plan, put out his lantern and went down the corridor counting each metre until he reached the wardrobe-closet door that led to the countess's chamber, where he expected a simple bolt to bar his way. But when he turned the knob it opened, and he told himself that fortune favoured him, and that to take the black pearl he need only be more silent than silence and more invisible than darkness. He spent a full half-hour opening the second door, a glass door to the bedchamber, with so much skill that even had the countess been awake she would not have heard the slightest sound.

He crept cautiously over the carpet, round the reclining chair, and paused to calm his heart, which throbbed like an alarm-bell, though no danger threatened him and he could not understand why a sleeping woman should move him so. He thought he heard her rhythmical breathing, which gave him confidence like a friend's presence, and feeling ahead with outstretched arm he reached the table, but his left hand met an overturned candlestick and then a small travelling clock. Suddenly a cry escaped him, for his hand had touched something strange and unutterable, and when he forced himself to feel again he found human hair and a human face, and the face was cold, almost icy.

However frightful the circumstances, a man like Lupin commands himself as soon as he knows what he faces, so he turned his lantern on the woman, and saw, as he leaned over her, that she was dead. He rose and turned on the electric lights, and saw all the marks of a desperate struggle, the bed in disorder, an overturned chair, and the little clock on the floor, with its hands at twenty minutes past eleven. He asked himself in a low voice about the black pearl, and opened the box of letter-paper, which stood in its place, but the jewel case inside was empty.

He told himself that he had boasted of his luck too soon, for with the countess dead and the pearl gone the situation was anything but pleasant, and he ought to leave before he got into serious trouble. Yet he did not move, for anyone else would have run, but Arsène Lupin had something better to do, and since his conscience was clear he would imagine himself the commissary of police conducting an inquiry. But to do that he needed a clearer head, for his own was muddled like a stew, and he fell into an armchair with his clenched hands pressed to his burning forehead.

Everyone in Paris knew the fair Léotine Zalti, the once-famous singer, wife and widow of the Count d'Andillot, whose luxury had dazzled the city twenty years earlier and whose diamonds and pearls were known across Europe. A catastrophe had swallowed her wealth, and of the whole marvellous collection nothing remained but the famous black pearl, which would have been a fortune if she had chosen to sell it. She preferred to live in a modest apartment with her companion, her cook and a manservant, for the pearl was the gift of an emperor, and she wore it by day and hid it at night where only she knew.

Two days later the newspapers announced the arrest of Victor Danègre, the countess's servant, in whose bed Dudouis had found a waistcoat with spots on the sleeve, while its missing button had been found beneath the victim's bed. It was supposed that he had seen the countess hide the pearl, but one point was obscure, for he had been to the tobacconist's at seven, although the doors were still locked when the cook and companion rose at eight. The question was how Danègre had left the apartment, and whether he had a second key, which was a matter for the police.

The investigation showed only that Danègre was a dangerous criminal, and new complications arose, for Mademoiselle de Sinclèves, the countess's heiress, said that a letter describing the pearl's hiding-place had vanished the day after she received it. The concierge spoke of the visitor who had asked for Doctor Harel, but the doctor said that nobody had rung his bell, so the public believed in an accomplice, as Ganimard did. Ganimard said that Lupin was at the bottom of it, but the judge answered that he saw Lupin everywhere, and that the clock showed eleven twenty, while the visitor came at three.

Officers of the law often form a hasty conviction and bend every discovery to fit it, and the judge, swayed by Danègre's bad record, closed his inquiry, so that the trial, a few weeks later, was slow and tedious. Danègre's counsel asked who had made the key without which the servant could not have locked the door behind him, who had seen the knife, and whether the clock's hands had been turned to deceive everyone. The prosecution had to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, he said, and it had not done so, and so Victor Danègre was acquitted.

Danègre left the prison on a Friday at dusk, weak and depressed by six months of captivity, for the questioning, the solitude and the trial had filled him with nervous fear, and at night he was tormented by terrible dreams. Under the false name of Anatole Dufour he rented a small room on the heights of Montmartre and lived by odd jobs, but three times he found regular work only to be recognised and discharged. Sometimes he fancied that men were following him, detectives who wished to trap and denounce him, and he could almost feel the strong hand of the law clutching him by the collar.

One evening, as Danègre dined in a neighbouring restaurant, a man of about forty in a doubtful coat sat at his table, gazed at him intently and raised his glass to the health of Victor Danègre. Danègre started in alarm and swore that his name was Dufour, but the stranger answered that he was Dufour to the proprietor and Danègre to the law, and gave him a card that read Grimaudan, ex-inspector. He was not from the police, he said, but was sent by Mademoiselle de Sinclèves, the heiress of the countess, to recover the black pearl that Danègre had stolen.

Danègre said with a forced smile that the jury had acquitted him unanimously, but the ex-inspector gripped his arm and told him to keep his fine phrases. Three weeks before the crime, he said, Danègre had taken the cook's key and had a copy made by a locksmith named Outard, and when Danègre cried that no such key existed, Grimaudan laid it on the table. Then he described the knife that Danègre had bought on the same day at the Bazar de la République, with a triangular blade, and when Danègre swore that nobody had seen it, he showed that too.

There was more evidence, Grimaudan said: in the wardrobe-closet, seized by fear, Danègre had leaned on the plaster wall, and the police, who never lit a candle to examine it, had missed the faint mark of his thumb. Under the Bertillon system, he added, thumb-marks are one of the principal means of identification, and Danègre, livid and sweating, gazed wildly at the man who had described his crime as if he had been an invisible witness. Overcome, he bowed his head and asked how much he would be paid for the pearl, and when the answer was nothing, only his life, he shuddered.

The pearl was worth nothing in his hands, Grimaudan said more gently, since he could not sell it, and the knife, the key and the thumb-mark would decide his fate if the police found him first. Danègre rested his head on his hands, feeling lost, and asked when he must give it up, and was told it must be that night, within the hour, or a letter from the heiress would go to the prosecutor. He poured out two glasses of wine, drank them quickly one after the other, and rising said that they should pay the bill and go, for he had had enough of the cursed affair.

Night had fallen, and the two men walked in silence down the rue Lepic and along the boulevards, Danègre stooping and dejected, until at the Parc Monceau he said dully that they were near the house. They passed the garden wall and the tobacconist's on the corner, and a few steps further Danègre sank, shaking, onto a bench and said that the pearl lay between two paving stones. Afraid of starving, he asked for enough money to buy a steerage ticket to America and a hundred francs to live on, and Grimaudan promised him two hundred if he spoke at once.

Danègre told him to count the paving stones to the right from the sewer-hole, and the pearl lay in the gutter, close to the sidewalk, between the twelfth and the thirteenth, ten centimetres down. Grimaudan glanced round, saw only passing trams and pedestrians, opened his pocketknife and thrust it between the stones, wondering whether a fortune could really lie in the mud of a gutter for the first comer to find. The point of the knife struck something, and he enlarged the hole with his finger and drew out the black pearl, then gave Danègre his two hundred francs and promised to send the ticket for America.

On the following day the Echo de France announced, and other newspapers repeated, that the famous black pearl had come to Arsène Lupin, who had recovered it from the countess's murderer. In a short time, it added, fac-similes of the precious jewel would be exhibited in London, Saint Petersburg, Calcutta, Buenos Ayres and New York, and Lupin would consider all propositions submitted through his agents. So the whole world learned that the black pearl, which the police had never found, now lay in the pocket of the gentleman-burglar.

Lupin told the writer that the forty minutes he spent in the apartment were the most thrilling of his life, for in them he calmly studied the scene and decided that a servant must be guilty. To get the pearl, he added, that servant had to be arrested, so he had left the button, carried away the knife and the key, locked the door and wiped the marks from the plaster. In an instant he had framed both halves of the problem, an arrest and an acquittal, and had used the machinery of the law to crush his victim until, once free, he would fall into the trap.

When the writer pitied Danègre, Lupin protested that the man might have sunk to the lowest depths of vice and crime if he had kept the pearl, whereas now he lived, and that was worth remembering. Then he took the pearl from a secret pocket of his wallet, examined it, gazed at it tenderly and caressed it with loving fingers, and he sighed. What cold Russian prince, he wondered, or what vain and foolish rajah, or perhaps what American millionaire, might one day own this morsel of exquisite beauty that had once adorned the bosom of Léotine Zalti?

At dinner in the Château de Thibermesnil, the banker Georges Devanne told his guest Horace Velmont that he bore a remarkable likeness to Arsène Lupin, whose photographs, no two alike, all gave the impression of a face like his. Velmont, the celebrated painter whose sea paintings Devanne admired, was vexed and said that he was not the first to notice it, but Devanne answered that only a cousin's recommendation had kept him from warning the police. The joke was greeted with laughter by the other guests, who included Father Gélis, the parish priest, and a dozen officers whose regiments were quartered in the neighbourhood.

An officer remarked that the police along the coast had a description of Arsène Lupin since his exploit on the Paris-Havre express, and Devanne replied that a week later he had met Velmont at the casino. Velmont had since honoured him with several visits, he said, an agreeable preamble to a more serious visit one of these days, or rather one of these nights, which provoked more laughter. The guests then passed into the ancient Hall of the Guards, a vast room with a high ceiling that filled the lower part of the Tour Guillaume, where Devanne had gathered the treasures of the lords of Thibermesnil.

The great hall held ancient chests, credences, andirons and chandeliers, its stone walls hung with magnificent tapestries, and its four Gothic windows were made of small panes of coloured glass set in lead. Between the door and the left window stood an immense Renaissance bookcase, and on its pediment, in letters of gold, were the word Thibermesnil and the proud family device, Do what thou wishest. When the guests had lit their cigars, Devanne told Velmont that he had no time to lose, for that night was his last chance, and Velmont, treating it as a joke, asked how that could be.

Devanne announced, with the satisfied air of a man with news, that tomorrow at four o'clock the famous English detective Sherlock Holmes, for whom mystery did not exist, would be his guest. The guests plied him with eager questions, and he answered that Lupin and his band were not far away, and that besides the robbery of Baron Cahorn he was credited with thefts at Montigny, Gruchet and Crasville. Now it was his own turn, he said, but there had been no warning letter this time, for Lupin could not work the same trick twice.

Devanne pointed to a gap between two folios and explained that a month earlier the Chronique de Thibermesnil, a sixteenth-century book with a sketch of a secret passage into this very room, had vanished from the shelf. There was another copy in the National Library in Paris, and the two differed in details of the passage, so that its exact place could be found only by comparing them. The day after his own book vanished, a reader called for the other one at the National Library and carried it away, and nobody knew how it was done.

The police, as usual, had found no clue, so Devanne had asked the help of Sherlock Holmes, who replied that he was ready and anxious to enter the lists against Arsène Lupin. On the chart the passage ended in a small circle marked T and G, for Tour Guillaume, but nobody knew the exact spot where it touched the round tower, which was surrounded by water. According to legend the lords of the castle had passed the secret from father to son on their deathbeds, until Geoffroy, the last of the race, was beheaded in the Revolution at nineteen, and the secret died with him.

Father Gélis, who loved to delve into the old archives, reminded them of two quotations, for two kings of France, Henry the Fourth and Louis the Sixteenth, were said to have known the key to the puzzle. According to the legend, Henry spent the night before the battle of Arques in the castle, and Duke Edgard brought the prettiest woman in Normandy, Louise de Tancarville, through the passage and told the king its secret. The king confided it to his minister Sully, who told the story in his memoirs and added, without comment, this puzzling line: turn one eye on the bee that shakes, the other eye will lead to God.

Devanne added that Louis the Sixteenth had stopped at the castle one night in 1784, and that a paper in the king's own writing, found in the famous Iron Casket at the Louvre, said Thibermesnil 3-4-11. Velmont laughed heartily that at last they had the magic key, and asked who could fit it to the invisible lock, and Devanne answered that Sherlock Holmes could, unless Lupin got ahead of him. Velmont rose, put his hand on Devanne's shoulder and thanked him for the missing key, adding that he must now plunder the castle that very night, before Sherlock Holmes arrived.

Devanne offered to drive Velmont to Dieppe that evening, since he was meeting Monsieur and Madame d'Androl and a young lady at the midnight train, and he asked the officers to breakfast the next day. The automobile left the artist at the casino and took Devanne to the station, and soon after midnight his friends were at the castle, where, after a light supper, they retired and the lights went out. The moon came and went behind the clouds, the clock struck two and then three, and suddenly something clicked, and a thin stream of light flashed from the central fluting of a column of the bookcase.

A section of the bookcase revolved on a pivot, disclosing an opening like a vault, and a man entered with an electric lantern, followed by another with ropes and tools, and then by eight stout fellows. Arsène Lupin went from one piece to another, deciding by its size and value whether to take it, and the chosen things, armchairs, Aubusson tapestries, candelabra, paintings by Fragonard and a bust by Houdon, were thrust into the tunnel. Sometimes he sighed that a fine chest or painting was too heavy, and in forty minutes the room was dismantled so quietly that everything might have been packed for the occasion.

Lupin told the last man out of the tunnel to take the auto-van, once loaded, to the grange at Roquefort, and asked only that the motor-cycle be left for himself. When the man had gone he pushed the bookcase back, carefully effaced the footprints, raised a curtain and entered the gallery, the only link between the tower and the castle. In the middle stood a glass cabinet of watches, snuff-boxes, rings and miniatures of rare workmanship, and he forced the lock with a small jimmy and filled a linen bag, specially prepared for such knick-knacks, and then his pockets.

He was hanging some pearl bags on his arm when he heard a slight sound, and he remembered that a stairway at the end of the gallery led to a room probably occupied by Devanne's young guest. He put out his lantern and slipped into a window recess as the door at the top of the stairs opened and a feeble light filled the gallery, and behind the curtain he sensed a woman coming cautiously down. She cried out faintly at the broken cabinet and came on toward the window, so close that her skirt brushed the curtain and he smelled her perfume, and then she hesitated, and suddenly drew the curtain aside.

They stood face to face, and Lupin was astounded, for it was Miss Nelly, who had haunted his dreams on that memorable voyage and who, rather than betray him, had dropped his Kodak into the water. They could neither move nor speak, hypnotised by the sudden sight of each other, and trembling with emotion she staggered to a seat while he stood before her. Gradually he realised how he must look, with his arms full of knick-knacks and his pockets overflowing, and he blushed like a thief caught in the act, then dropped everything into an armchair.

She shuddered and fled toward the salon, where she stood trembling at the sight of the devastated room, and he followed and promised that tomorrow at three o'clock everything would be returned, the furniture included. A long silence followed, and he turned away quietly, thinking that he could not bear her presence, when she suddenly stammered that she heard footsteps and that he must escape. He looked at her in astonishment, for he heard nothing, but she ran to the gallery door and listened, and when she returned, reassured, Arsène Lupin had vanished.

As soon as Devanne learned of the pillage he told himself that Velmont had done it and that Velmont was Arsène Lupin, but it seemed so preposterous that he did not mention it to the gendarmes. All morning the castle was in lively commotion, with gendarmes, police and villagers in every hall, but there was no clue, for doors and windows were undisturbed and the goods must have left by the secret passage. They did find one curious proof of Lupin's whimsical character: the sixteenth-century Chronique had been put back in its usual place, and beside it stood the volume stolen from the National Library.

At eleven the officers arrived, and Devanne welcomed them gaily, for his great wealth let him bear the loss philosophically, and he introduced Monsieur and Madame d'Androl and Miss Nelly, though one expected guest, Horace Velmont, was missing. At twelve Velmont arrived, and Devanne cried that he had robbed the castle, as predicted, and then, seeing Miss Nelly's extreme agitation, supposed that she, who had met Arsène Lupin on the steamer, was struck by the resemblance. She did not reply, but Velmont, smiling, bowed and offered his arm, and escorted her to the table, where he sat opposite her.

Coffee was served on the terrace above the flower garden, where the regimental band played on the lawn and soldiers and peasants wandered through the park, but Nelly had not forgotten for a moment Lupin's solemn promise. The great clock in the right wing marked twenty minutes to three, and in spite of herself her eyes went to it every minute, and to Velmont, who was calmly swinging in a comfortable rocking chair. Could he really keep his promise with the castle full of people and the police at work, yet his assurance had so impressed her that it seemed to her a natural event, not a miracle?

The great clock struck three, Velmont glanced at his watch, and a few seconds later the crowd in the courtyard parted for two army wagons that stopped before the main entrance. A sergeant leaped down and asked for Monsieur Devanne, who found under the canvas covers all his furniture and ornaments, carefully packed. The sergeant had an order, signed Colonel Beauvel, to collect the goods at the crossroads of Halleux and bring them at three, and although an officer called the signature a clever forgery, everything was put back.

Nelly stood alone at the end of the terrace when Velmont came close and asked softly whether he had not kept his promise, but she did not answer. He reminded her of the white rose she had left on the deck of the Provence, and begged her to look at him as she had looked at Bernard. She raised her eyes and, without a word, pointed to the magnificent ruby on his forefinger, which was Devanne's, and he blushed and said that she was right, that nothing could be changed.

She passed before him and entered the house, and he wished to hold her back and beg her pardon, but his courage failed, and he followed her with his eyes, as he had on the gangway at New York. A cloud hid the sun, and then he started, for on the flower box where she had stood lay the white rose he had wanted and dared not ask for, forgotten, perhaps, or left on purpose. He seized it eagerly, gathered up the petals that fell from it like precious relics, and told himself that he must think of his safety before Sherlock Holmes arrived.

The park was deserted but for some gendarmes at the gate, so Lupin entered a grove of pines, leaped over the wall and followed a path across the fields, as a short cut to the railway station. After walking about ten minutes he came to a spot where the road narrowed and ran between two steep banks, and in this ravine he met a man traveling in the opposite direction. He was about fifty years old, tall and smooth-shaven, dressed in clothes of foreign cut, and he carried a heavy cane and a small satchel strapped across his shoulder.

The stranger asked in a slight English accent whether this was the way to the castle, and Lupin said that it was straight ahead and that they expected Sherlock Holmes, who had no more ardent admirer than himself. There was a touch of irony in his voice that he quickly regretted, for the stranger scrutinised him from head to foot so keenly that he felt seized, imprisoned and registered more thoroughly than by any camera. His negative was taken now, he thought, and a disguise would be useless against such a man, but he wondered whether he had been recognised.

They bowed as if to part, but then they heard horses' feet and clinking steel, and both men had to step back against the bank among the bushes while a line of gendarmes passed, one after another. Lupin thought that everything depended on whether Holmes had recognised him, for if so he would surely seize the chance, and when the last horseman had passed the two men gazed at each other for a long moment. Then Holmes brushed the dust from his clothes and said, “Thank you, monsieur,” and Lupin answered that he was quite welcome, and they parted, one for the station, the other for the castle.

The people at the castle awaited the English detective with lively curiosity, and at first sight they were a little disappointed by his commonplace appearance, so unlike the romantic hero of their imaginations. Devanne welcomed him gladly, but the Englishman, who had come by train instead of using the car sent to meet him, grumbled that he did not like official receptions with music and fireworks. When Devanne told him that the robbery had taken place the night before, Holmes replied that if his visit had not been announced, it would not have happened then, and Lupin would have been trapped.

Holmes put on his cap and said that he was going home, since the goods were back and Lupin was far away, but Devanne begged him to stay, for they did not know how Lupin had come and gone. The idea of a problem quickened his interest, and in a dry, crisp voice he questioned Devanne about the guests, examined the two volumes of the Chronique, compared the plans and had the two sentences repeated. Learning that Velmont had first heard them the night before, he ordered the automobile within the hour, for Lupin, who was Velmont, had solved the problem in that time.

Holmes paced the room in deep thought, then sat down with his eyes closed, and when Devanne returned from giving some orders he found him on his knees, studying the carpet at the foot of the gallery stairs. There were fresh candle spots, and he said they would also be found at the top of the stairs and by the broken cabinet, and doubtless explained why the goods had been returned. But that was a side issue, he said, since the passage came first, and when Devanne spoke of a ruined chapel with the tomb of Duke Rollo, Holmes asked for a ladder and a lantern.

Holmes had the ladder placed to the left of the word Thibermesnil and told Devanne to climb up and turn the first letter I, which, to his surprise, turned toward the right. He told him to move the letter B like a bolt, which produced a click, and then to try the last letter I at the other end of the word, to see whether it opened like a wicket. Devanne seized it with some solemnity, and it opened, but he fell from the ladder, for the entire section of the bookcase between the first and last letters turned on a pivot and disclosed the subterranean passage.

Holmes said that this agreed exactly with Sully's formula, and explained that Louis the Sixteenth, a clever locksmith who had written a book on combination locks, had noted 3-4-11 to remember the third, fourth and eleventh letters of the word. Lighting his lantern, he stepped into the passage, where all the mechanism lay exposed like the works of a clock, and a puddle of oil proved that Lupin had worked the combination from this side. They descended twelve steps, then twelve more, and two other flights, and walked along a long passage of old brick that dripped with water, so that Devanne said nervously that they were passing under the pond.

At the top they found a small cavity in the rock and bare walls, until Holmes saw the same mechanism and the same word and worked the three letters, and a block of granite swung aside. Its other side was the tombstone of Duke Rollo, and they stood in the ruined chapel, which was what the eye that leads to God had meant, though the cross on the chart had been enough for Holmes. An automobile waited outside, and the chauffeur Edouard told Devanne that Monsieur Velmont had met him near the station and told him to wait there for his master and his friend.

Holmes said that he had met Lupin on the road and let him go, since with such an adversary he did not take advantage of chance opportunities but created them. In the car they found a small package addressed to Sherlock Holmes, from Arsène Lupin, and it held the detective's own watch, which Lupin had somehow taken, and Devanne roared with laughter. The Englishman never moved a muscle on the way to Dieppe, but at the station he vowed that the world was too small, and that some day he and Arsène Lupin would meet again.
